sections.results:
In the HDM-induced murine asthma model, immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis showed significantly reduced BMAL1 expression in the airway epithelium compared to the control group (A). In vitro, HDM stimulation of HBE cells resulted in a dose-dependent decrease in BMAL1 protein levels, with more pronounced reductions at higher concentrations (400 and 800 U/mL) compared with controls (B and C).

To assess the pathological consequences of BMAL1 deficiency in vivo, we established an HDM-induced asthma model in wild-type (WT) and Bmal1 -knockout ( Bmal1 -ko) mice (D). HDM challenge induced typical asthmatic pathology in WT mice, including airway inflammatory infiltration, mucus hypersecretion, and peribronchial collagen deposition. These changes were further exacerbated in Bmal1 -ko mice, as evidenced by increased inflammatory cell accumulation on H&E staining, enhanced goblet cell metaplasia on PAS staining, and increased collagen deposition on Masson's trichrome staining (E–G). BALF analysis supported these histological observations.

Consistently, BALF analysis showed increased total inflammatory cell counts in Bmal1- ko + HDM mice compared with WT + HDM controls, along with elevated eosinophils, neutrophils, and lymphocytes (H–K). In parallel, Bmal1 -ko + HDM mice exhibited higher levels of the Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13), as well as the epithelial alarmins (IL-25 and IL-33), whereas TSLP was not significantly changed (L and M). HDM-specific IgE was also further increased (N). Together, these findings demonstrate that BMAL1 deficiency exacerbates HDM-induced airway inflammation and remodeling.

To explore the molecular basis underlying the aggravated asthmatic phenotype, we performed transcriptomic and untargeted metabolomic analyses of lung tissues from HDM-treated WT and Bmal1 -ko mice (A). Transcriptomic profiling revealed widespread gene expression changes, with 1434 upregulated and 916 downregulated genes in Bmal1 -ko + HDM lungs compared with WT + HDM controls (B). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis showed significant enrichment of immune and inflammatory processes (C), while KEGG analysis identified significant enrichment of multiple pro-inflammatory pathways, including cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, NOD-like receptor signaling, chemokine signaling, and JAK-STAT signaling (D), consistent with the aggravated airway inflammatory phenotype observed in Bmal1 -ko mice.

Metabolomic analysis further demonstrated clear separation between groups by PLS-DA (E), with 120 upregulated and 37 downregulated metabolites identified in Bmal1 -ko + HDM lungs (F). KEGG pathway analysis revealed enrichment of ferroptosis, glycerophospholipid metabolism, and biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids (G). Consistently, heatmap analysis of metabolites further showed coordinated changes in metabolites associated with lipid peroxidation, unsaturated fatty acid metabolism, and glutathione metabolism (H). Notably, metabolites associated with polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism and glutathione homeostasis were reduced, whereas oxidized lipid species were increased, indicating disrupted lipid redox homeostasis.

Collectively, these data indicate that BMAL1 deficiency is associated with enhanced inflammatory activation and ferroptosis-related metabolic reprogramming in lungs. We next examined whether ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury was increased in vivo.

Based on the multi-omics findings, we assessed ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury in vivo. Immunohistochemical analysis showed GPX4, a key ferroptosis suppressor, was reduced in the airway epithelium after HDM exposure and was further decreased in Bmal1 -ko mice (A). In contrast, COX2, a ferroptosis-related protein, was upregulated after HDM treatment and displayed stronger staining in the airway epithelium of Bmal1 -ko mice (B). In parallel, 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), a marker of lipid peroxidation, accumulated in the airway epithelium following HDM exposure and was further accentuated in Bmal1 -ko mice (C), indicating enhanced lipid peroxidation in the absence of BMAL1. Consistently, lung MDA levels were further elevated in Bmal1 -ko mice compared with WT controls (D). Western blot analysis confirmed decreased GPX4 and xCT protein levels and increased COX2 expression after HDM treatment, with more marked alterations in Bmal1 -ko mice (E and ). Together, these data indicate that BMAL1 deficiency exacerbates HDM-induced ferroptosis-associated molecular changes and lipid peroxidation in the airway epithelium in vivo.

To determine the functional relevance of ferroptosis, mice were treated with Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) during HDM exposure (F). Histological examination demonstrated that Fer-1 improved airway histopathology, with reduced peribronchial inflammatory cell infiltration, mucus production, and collagen deposition (). BALF analysis showed decreased total inflammatory cell counts and reduced eosinophils, neutrophils, and lymphocytes in Bmal1 -ko mice with Fer-1 treatment (J). Fer-1 treatment also attenuated ferroptosis-associated changes, as indicated by reduced MDA levels (K), increased GPX4 and xCT protein levels, and decreased COX2 expression (L and ). Consistent with these biochemical changes, immunohistochemistry showed partial restoration of GPX4 expression and reduced COX2 and 4-HNE signals in the airway epithelium (M–O). Collectively, these findings support that BMAL1 deficiency aggravates HDM-induced airway injury through enhanced epithelial ferroptosis, whereas pharmacological inhibition of ferroptosis alleviates both molecular alterations and airway pathology.

To define whether BMAL1 deficiency directly sensitized epithelial cells to HDM, we established a BMAL1-deficient HBE cell model. Efficient knockdown of BMAL1 in HBE cells was confirmed at both protein and mRNA levels (A and B). CCK8 assay showed that HDM exposure reduced cell viability, which was further exacerbated by BMAL1 deficiency (C). Moreover, measurement of MDA indicated that HDM increased lipid peroxidation in HBE cells, with a greater accumulation observed under BMAL1-deficient conditions (D). Assessment of lipid peroxidation using BODIPY 581/591 C11 staining further demonstrated that HDM enhanced lipid oxidation, and this response was accentuated by BMAL1 knockdown (E). Intracellular ROS levels were also increased in BMAL1-deficient cells after HDM stimulation (F). Western blot further showed that HDM exposure reduced GPX4 and xCT protein levels while elevating COX2 abundance, with more pronounced alterations in BMAL1-deficient cells (G–J). Together, these data indicate that BMAL1 deficiency enhances susceptibility to HDM-induced ferroptotic stress in airway epithelial cells.

To assess the functional role of ferroptosis, BMAL1-deficient cells were treated with Fer-1. Fer-1 partially restored cell viability under HDM stimulation (K) and reduced lipid peroxidation, as shown by decreased MDA levels and BODIPY fluorescence (L and M). Intracellular ROS levels were also attenuated under BMAL1-deficient conditions (N). Consistently, Fer-1 increased GPX4 and xCT protein levels while reducing COX2 expression in HDM-stimulated BMAL1-deficient cells (O–R). Overall, these results demonstrate that the susceptibility conferred by BMAL1 loss is directly mediated by the ferroptosis pathway and is responsive to Fer-1 treatment.

Given the exacerbation of HDM-induced airway injury by BMAL1 deficiency, we next assessed whether AAV6-mediated BMAL1 overexpression altered the response to HDM in vivo. An AAV6 vector encoding BMAL1 was delivered by airway instillation, and efficient overexpression in the lung was confirmed (). The experimental design is shown in . Unexpectedly, BMAL1 overexpression did not confer protection but instead exacerbated airway pathology. Histological analysis revealed increased peribronchial and perivascular inflammatory infiltration (H&E), enhanced mucus production (PAS), and greater collagen deposition (Masson's trichrome) (). Moreover, BALF analysis further showed elevated total inflammatory cell counts, along with increased eosinophils, neutrophils, and lymphocytes in the BMAL1-overexpression group (). These results showed that BMAL1 overexpression failed to protect against HDM-induced injury and instead aggravated airway inflammation and remodeling.

As constitutive BMAL1 overexpression was not protective, we next turned to melatonin as a more physiological circadian intervention. In addition to its role as a key circadian output signal, melatonin has well-established antioxidant and redox-modulating properties []. To evaluate a physiological circadian intervention, we examined the effects of melatonin in redox homeostasis in HDM-induced asthma.

We first explored its effect in a standard HDM-induced asthma model in wild-type mice (). Serum melatonin levels were significantly reduced after HDM exposure, consistent with potential circadian disruption under allergic inflammation (). Melatonin administration attenuated airway pathology, including inflammatory infiltration, mucus production, and remodeling, and reduced BALF inflammatory cells, Th2 cytokines, epithelial alarmins, and serum IgE levels (). Furthermore, melatonin suppressed ferroptosis-associated changes in vivo, as indicated by the recovery of GPX4 and xCT protein expression and the reductions in COX2 and 4-HNE levels in lung tissues ().

Moreover, in HDM-stimulated HBE cells, melatonin improved cell viability and reduced ROS accumulation, lipid peroxidation (BODIPY staining and MDA levels), and COX2 expression, while restoring GPX4 and xCT levels (). These findings showed that melatonin alleviated HDM-induced ferroptosis-related changes in airway epithelial cells.

We next assessed whether melatonin could rescue the aggravated phenotype in Bmal1 -ko mice (A). Melatonin markedly attenuated airway inflammation, goblet cell metaplasia, and remodeling (B–D), accompanied by reduced BALF inflammatory cells (E–H). This protective effect was associated with reduced epithelial ferroptosis, as evidenced by decreased 4-HNE and COX2 levels, and restored GPX4 expression in epithelial cells (I). In parallel, ferroptosis-associated changes in lung tissues were also reduced, as shown by lower MDA levels and restored GPX4 and xCT expression together with reduced COX2 abundance in Bmal1 -ko mice (J–L). Taken together, these data demonstrated that melatonin ameliorated the exacerbated allergic airway inflammation driven by BMAL1 deficiency, an effect closely linked to the suppression of epithelial ferroptosis.

To define the mechanism by which BMAL1 deficiency promotes ferroptosis, we performed RNA sequencing in HDM-stimulated HBE cells with or without BMAL1 knockdown. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed significant activation of the AP-1 pathway upon BMAL1 knockdown (A and B). Among AP-1 components, JUN protein levels were selectively increased, whereas c-FOS remained unchanged (C and D). Consistently, immunofluorescence staining showed enhanced JUN accumulation in the airway epithelium of HDM-exposed Bmal1 -ko mice (E).

Because COX2 (encoded by PTGS2) emerged as a recurrent downstream change under BMAL1-deficient conditions, we next assessed prostaglandin metabolism. Metabolomic analysis showed increased levels of prostaglandin G2 (PGG2) among the altered metabolites (F), and ELISA confirmed elevated prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) in Bmal1 -ko + HDM lungs (G), indicating activation of the COX2-dependent prostaglandin pathway.

Analysis of the PTGS2 promoter identified a conserved JUN-binding motif (H). Cut&Tag-qPCR further demonstrated increased JUN occupancy at the PTGS2 promoter in BMAL1-deficient HBE cells under HDM stimulation (I).

Furthermore, melatonin treatment reduced JUN expression in HBE cells and attenuated JUN accumulation in the airway epithelium of Bmal1 -ko mice, whereas c-FOS remained unchanged ().

Together, these data identify JUN as a key transcriptional mediator downstream of BMAL1 deficiency, linking BMAL1 loss to JUN-associated COX2 induction and ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury.

To assess the functional role of JUN signaling, HDM-challenged Bmal1 -ko mice were treated with the JUN inhibitor SP600125 (A). Histological analysis showed that SP600125 markedly attenuated airway pathology, as reflected by reduced inflammatory cell infiltration (H&E), decreased mucus production (PAS), and diminished collagen deposition (Masson's trichrome) (B–D). BALF analysis showed a reduction in total inflammatory cell counts after SP600125 treatment (E).

Consistently, SP600125 suppressed ferroptosis-associated changes in vivo. Immunofluorescence demonstrated reduced JUN accumulation (F), while immunohistochemistry showed decreased 4-HNE and COX2 levels and restored GPX4 expression in the airway epithelium (G). Western blot analysis further confirmed increased GPX4 and xCT expression and reduced COX2 abundance (H). These in vivo findings supported a role for JUN signaling in linking BMAL1 deficiency to oxidative lipid damage and ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury.

To determine whether JUN suppression exerted similar effects in vitro, BMAL1-deficient HBE cells exposed to HDM were treated with SP600125. SP600125 reduced lipid peroxidation (BODIPY staining) and intracellular ROS levels (I and J), and partially reversed ferroptosis-associated molecular changes, as indicated by increased GPX4 and xCT and decreased COX2 and JUN expression (K and L). Collectively, these findings indicate that JUN inhibition mitigates ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury and airway inflammation under BMAL1-deficient conditions, supporting a functional role for JUN signaling in the BMAL1-deficient phenotype and suggesting that COX2 induction is a downstream JUN-associated response.
sections.discussion:
Although inhaled corticosteroid-based therapy remains central to asthma management, a subset of patients remains poorly controlled, with persistent symptoms, recurrent exacerbations, and progressive airway remodeling []. These challenges highlight the need to define mechanisms of disease persistence and identify additional therapeutic targets. Asthma pathogenesis involves multicellular interactions, and epithelial dysfunction is a key determinant of ongoing inflammation and remodeling in asthma [,]. Although circadian disruption is a known risk factor for asthma exacerbations and poor disease control [,], its molecular link to epithelial injury via clock gene dysregulation is unclear. In this study, we identified the core clock component BMAL1 as a critical regulator of airway epithelial vulnerability and placed ferroptosis-associated injury downstream of circadian disruption. BMAL1 deficiency aggravated airway pathology together with enhanced lipid peroxidation, impaired antioxidant defense, and a broader ferroptosis-related epithelial phenotype. Multi-omics analyses further revealed inflammatory activation and lipid metabolic remodeling, while activation of the JUN/COX2 axis was linked to this injury program. Functional rescue by ferroptosis inhibition, JUN suppression, and melatonin supports the contribution of ferroptosis-associated lipid peroxidation and JUN signaling to allergic airway pathology.

Asthma exhibits marked circadian variation, and altered clock gene expression has been reported in airway epithelial cells from asthmatic donors []. Previous studies support a protective role for BMAL1 in airway inflammation and glucocorticoid responsiveness [,]. Our findings extend these observations by showing that circadian dysregulation contributes directly to asthma pathobiology. We found that BMAL1 deficiency aggravated HDM-induced airway inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and remodeling, accompanied by inflammatory activation and lipid metabolic reprogramming consistent with a ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury program. These results suggest that BMAL1-dependent circadian regulation contributes to epithelial redox homeostasis and limits susceptibility to ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury during allergic airway inflammation.

Notably, the biological effect of BMAL1 appears to depend on properly timed circadian regulation rather than expression abundance alone. An unexpected observation in our study was that BMAL1 overexpression also aggravated HDM-induced asthma, despite the detrimental effect of BMAL1 deficiency. This finding argues against a simple linear protective role of BMAL1 and instead suggests that airway protection requires tightly regulated circadian homeostasis. BMAL1 normally functions within a rhythmic feedback loop, in which disruption of its amplitude or phase may disturb coordinated circadian output []. Sustained BMAL1 overexpression may therefore induce transcriptional imbalance by interfering with this rhythmic regulation. Similar bidirectional effects have been observed for other clock components []. These findings highlight the importance of circadian precision rather than absolute BMAL1 abundance, which should be considered when developing therapeutic strategies targeting the clock.

Ferroptosis has emerged as an important component of airway epithelial injury in asthma. Multiple pathways, including ferritinophagy-dependent iron mobilization [], PEBP1-mediated lipid peroxidation [], ALOX15/15LO1-driven phospholipid oxidation [,], and IL-13-induced SLC7A11 suppression [], have been implicated. The SLC7A11/xCT-GSH-GPX4 axis represents a central antioxidant defense against ferroptosis by supporting glutathione-dependent detoxification of lipid hydroperoxides [,]. Lipid metabolism is tightly linked to ferroptosis, as phospholipid remodeling and oxidation govern lipid peroxide accumulation [,]; thus, ferroptosis inhibition could attenuate cellular lipid peroxidation []. Our data suggest that BMAL1 deficiency increases susceptibility to ferroptosis, as evidenced by enhanced lipid peroxidation, reduced GPX4/xCT-mediated antioxidant defense, and rescue by ferroptosis inhibition in epithelial cells. Metabolomic changes in polyunsaturated fatty acid and glutathione pathways further support a ferroptosis-prone state. Consistent with this, studies in other diseases have identified BMAL1 as a regulator of ferroptosis sensitivity. Reduced BMAL1 activity has been linked to enhanced hepatocyte ferroptosis in metabolic liver disease [], BMAL1-dependent antioxidant programs protect against ethanol-induced ferroptotic injury [], and studies in acute myeloid leukemia have connected BMAL1 to ferroptosis control through the EBF3/ALOX15 axis and HMGB1-GPX4 signaling [,]. Together, these observations support BMAL1 as an upstream determinant of ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury in asthma.

AP-1/JUN is a stress-responsive transcription factor known to regulate COX2 expression [, , ]. COX2 (PTGS2) catalyzes prostaglandin synthesis from arachidonic acid, thereby linking lipid metabolism to inflammatory signaling [, , ]. This is relevant because ferroptosis is driven by polyunsaturated phospholipids peroxidation, with arachidonic acid-derived phospholipids as major substrates [,]. In our study, we showed that BMAL1 deficiency activated AP-1 signaling with selective JUN upregulation, enhanced JUN binding at the PTGS2 promoter, and increased PGG2 and PGE2 levels, indicating activation of the JUN/COX2 axis in epithelial cells. Inhibition of JUN reduced COX2 expression, lipid peroxidation, and ROS accumulation while restoring GPX4 and xCT. Our data support JUN signaling as a functionally relevant downstream pathway linking BMAL1 deficiency to ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury, with COX2 induction representing a potential downstream effector of JUN. This is consistent with previous studies showing that modulation of PTGS2(COX2) affects ferroptotic responses []. In addition, enhanced COX2-dependent flux through the PGG2/PGH2 intermediate pool may alter the balance of downstream prostanoids, including potentially protective PGE2 signaling and remodeling-associated mediators such as PGD2 []. This shift could influence epithelial-smooth muscle communication and contribute to airway smooth muscle-associated remodeling, although smooth muscle remodeling and broader prostanoid profiles were not directly assessed in this study. More broadly, BMAL1 loss also altered inflammatory activation, lipid metabolism, antioxidant defense, and circadian-redox homeostasis. Thus, JUN/COX2 signaling likely contributes to the ferroptosis-related epithelial phenotype as part of a broader redox and metabolic disturbance associated with BMAL1 deficiency.

Melatonin attenuated airway inflammation and ferroptosis-associated injury in our study. As a circadian hormone with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties [, , ], melatonin restored GPX4 and xCT expression, reduced COX2, 4-HNE, and MDA levels, and suppressed JUN activation. The observation that melatonin remained protective in Bmal1-deficient mice, whereas constitutive BMAL1 overexpression was not beneficial, suggests that its effects are unlikely to depend solely on increasing BMAL1 abundance. Instead, the beneficial effects of melatonin may involve partial restoration of circadian-redox homeostasis and attenuation of lipid peroxidation, thereby reducing susceptibility to ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury during allergic airway inflammation. These findings suggest a potential role for melatonin as a chronobiotic and redox-modulating strategy in allergic airway disease, while emphasizing that clock-targeted interventions may need to restore circadian-redox balance rather than simply enhance BMAL1 expression.

Nevertheless, several issues should be considered when interpreting these findings. Although ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury was supported by changes in GPX4, xCT, COX2, 4-HNE, MDA, lipid ROS, and Ferrostatin-1 rescue, iron accumulation or labile iron levels were not directly measured. Future studies incorporating direct iron detection would further strengthen the assessment of iron-dependent lipid peroxidation. COX2 was markedly upregulated under BMAL1-deficient conditions and appeared to be regulated by JUN; however, COX2-specific inhibition was not performed in this study. Thus, COX2 may represent a potential downstream effector of JUN, but its functional requirement in this pathway remains to be further validated using selective COX2 inhibition or PTGS2 genetic suppression. Moreover, the in vivo experiments were performed in global Bmal1 -knockout mice rather than epithelial-specific deletion models, and the in vitro experiments used immortalized HBE135-E6E7 cells instead of primary airway epithelial cultures. Constitutive BMAL1 overexpression also does not fully reproduce physiological circadian oscillation. Future studies using complementary epithelial subset-specific Bmal1 deletion models, time-resolved approaches, and primary human bronchial epithelial cells or airway samples will help further clarify the cell-type specificity and clinical relevance of BMAL1-dependent ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury.

In conclusion, we identify BMAL1 as a critical regulator of airway epithelial ferroptosis in allergic asthma. BMAL1 deficiency promotes HDM-induced airway inflammation and remodeling in parallel with increased lipid peroxidation, impaired antioxidant defense, activation of JUN signaling, and COX2-associated prostaglandin responses. The ability of ferroptosis inhibition, JUN inhibition, and melatonin to attenuate this aggravated phenotype further supports a functional link between circadian disruption and epithelial redox injury. Together with the observation that constitutive BMAL1 overexpression was not beneficial, these findings suggest that maintenance of circadian-redox homeostasis is critical for airway protection and provides a rationale for targeting ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury in allergic airway disease.
sections.methods:
HDM was purchased from ALK-Abello A/S (Denmark). The preparation used was Alutard SQ, ALK 503 D.p, a Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus -derived, partially purified and standardized HDM allergen extract adsorbed to aluminum hydroxide, with a maintenance concentration of 100000 SQ-U/ml (Lot No. M5271). Ferrostatin-1 (HY-100579), Melatonin (HY–B0075), SP600125 (HY-12041) were purchased from MedChemExpress. Other reagents were described below.

The human bronchial epithelial cell line HBE135-E6E7 (ATCC, USA) was used in this study. HBE cells were cultured in KM (ScienCell, USA) at 37 °C in a humidified 5% CO 2 incubator. Transfection of siRNA was performed using Lipo3000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were transiently transfected with BMAL1-targeting siRNA or scrambled siRNA negative control (NC) designed by JinKaiRui Genecreate (China). BMAL1 knockdown efficiency was confirmed 24 h after transfection before downstream assays at both the mRNA and protein levels by qRT-PCR and western blot, respectively, as shown in A and B. The siRNA target sequences used in this study are as follows: BMAL1 (sense, 5'-ACGCGAUAGAUGGAAAGUUTT-3'; antisense, 5'-AACUUUCCAUCUAUCGCGUTT-3'). In the follow-up experiment, cells were treated with small interfering RNA (siRNA), Ferrostatin-1 (5 μM), Melatonin (200 μM), SP600125 (10 μM) before being exposed to HDM.

Cell and tissue lysates were prepared in ice-cold RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. After centrifugation, protein concentrations in the supernatants were determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit (BL521A, Biosharp), and equal amounts of protein were analyzed by western blot. Samples were boiled with 5×loading buffer and separated by 8-12% sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE). Separated proteins were transferred to 0.22 μm polyvinylidene fluoride membranes and blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin for 1h at room temperature. Afterwards, the membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C on a shaker with primary antibodies including antibodies against the BMAL1/ARNTL (14268-1-AP, Proteintech), GPX4 (A25009, ABclonal), SLC7A11/xCT ( A24113 , ABclonal), COX2 (27308-1-AP, Proteintech), JUN (24909-1-AP, Proteintech), c-FOS (YM4385, Immunoway), β-actin (66009-1-IG, Proteintech), GAPDH (10494-1-AP, Proteintech). After three washes with TBS-T buffer (5 min each), the membranes were incubated with fluorescence-labeled secondary antibodies (LI-COR) for 1 h at room temperature. Protein bands were scanned using LI-COR Odyssey System.

C57BL/6J wild-type mice (6-8 weeks old, 18-22 g, SPF grade) were purchased from the Animal Experimental Center of Southern Medical University (Guangzhou, China). Bmal1 heterozygous mice ( Bmal1 +/− mice) were provided by View Solid Biotech (China). Bmal1 −/− ( Bmal1 -ko) mice and Bmal1 +/+ (Wild-Type, WT) mice were confirmed by genotyping of ear tissue. Genotyping was performed via PCR using primers OL2646:5'-CCACCAAGCCCAGCAACTCA-3'; OL2647:5'-ATTCGGCCCCCTATCTTCTGC-3'; and OL278:5'-TCGCCTTCTATCGCCTTCTTCTTGACG-3'. The results of the PCR identification are shown in the Supplementary Figure (). All animals were housed in the Laboratory Animal Center of Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University. Mice were maintained in standard environment with a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle, with lights on at 07:00 and lights off at 19:00, and had free access to water and food. Zeitgeber time 0 (ZT0) was defined as the time of lights on. All experiments were approved by the Ethics Committee for Animal Experimentation of Southern Medical University and performed in accordance with institutional guidelines.

For the experimental asthma model, mice were intraperitoneally sensitized with allergen mixture containing HDM (4000U/mice) on day 0 and day 7, and were challenged by intranasal administration of the HDM (800U/mice) daily for 14 days (day 8-day 21). All HDM sensitizations and intranasal challenges were performed at a fixed time of day, between 08:00 and 10:00, corresponding to ZT1-ZT3. Control mice received an equivalent volume of PBS at the same time of day. For the intervention groups, mice were intraperitoneally injected with Ferrostatin-1 (5 mg/kg), Melatonin (10 mg/kg), or SP600125 (30 mg/kg) 1 h prior to each HDM challenge. All the mice were sacrificed 24 h after the final HDM challenge for further analysis.

Recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 6 (AAV6) vectors encoding BMAL1 (AAV6-BMAL1, for overexpression) and the corresponding empty control vector were sourced from WZ Biosciences Inc (Shandong, China). The vectors were provided at a titer of 1.05 × 10 13 vg/ml, and each mouse received 5 × 10 11 vg of the respective AAV6 vector by intratracheal instillation. Two weeks after vector administration, the mice were subjected to induction of the experimental asthma model.

Lung tissues were isolated, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and embedded in paraffin. For histological analysis, lung sections were subjected to hematoxylin and eosin (HE, BL700B, Biosharp), periodic acid-Schiff (PAS, G1281, Solarbio), Masson's trichrome (G1346, Solarbio) staining according to the manufacturer's protocols. The degree of inflammatory infiltration was scored as described previously: 0 = no inflammatory cells; 1 = sparse infiltration; 2 = inflammatory cell ring (1 cell layer thick); 3 = inflammatory cell ring (2-4 cell layers thick); 4 = inflammatory cell ring (>4 cell layers thick). For immunohistochemical staining, lung sections were incubated with primary antibodies against BMAL1 (1:200, ABclonal), 4-HNE (1:400, MedChemExpress), GPX4 (1:500, ABclonal), COX2 (1:400, Immunoway) respectively. Sections were incubated with biotinylated goat anti-rabbit secondary antibodies (consistent with the DAB substrate kit, Zhong Shan Jin Qiao) in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. Representative images of lung sections were captured by light microscopy.

Paraffin sections of lung tissue (4 μm) were incubated overnight at 4 °C with the following primary antibodies: COX2 (1:200, 27308-1-AP, Proteintech), JUN (1:200, YM8321, Immunoway) and stained with Alexa Fluor 594 Donkey anti-Rabbit IgG (H + L) secondary antibody (A-21207, Invitrogen) at room temperature for 1 h, after which nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (MedChemExpress). Images were obtained using a fluorescence microscope (TissueFAXS, Austria).

Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was collected by lavaging the lungs with sterile PBS. Total BALF cells were counted using an automated cell counter (Countstar, China). For differential counts, BALF cells were prepared by cytospin centrifugation, stained with Wright-Giemsa staining solution, and classified according to the morphology-based cytological criteria described by Kalidhindi et al. []. At least 200 cells per sample were counted by investigators blinded to the experimental groups. Samples with obvious blood contamination or inadequate cytospin quality were excluded from differential analysis.

The levels of IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IL-33, and TSLP in BALF were measured using ELISA kits (Proteintech), whereas IL-25 was determined by ELISA (UpingBio). Serum HDM-specific IgE and melatonin levels were measured by ELISA (Gelatins). All assays were performed according to the manufacturers’ instructions.

For the assessment of cell viability, HBE cells were subjected to the Cell Counting Kit-8 assay (CK04, DOJINDO) according to the manufacturer's protocol.

Levels of Malondialdehyde were determined using the MDA Assay Kit (S0131S, Beyotime) in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions.

The reactive oxygen species assay kit (DCFH-DA) was purchased from Beyotime (S0033S). Briefly, cells were loaded with DCFH-DA (1:1000) and were incubated in the dark at 37 °C for 20 min. Cells were then gently washed three times, and images were captured using a fluorescence microscope ( N31373 , Nikon, Japan).

Lipid peroxidation was measured using the Assay Kit with BODIPY 581/591 C11 (S0043S, Beyotime). In brief, cells were incubated for 30 min at 37 °C in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) supplemented with BODIPY 581/591 C11 probe (2 μM) and protected from light. After washing with PBS three times, cells were photographed under a confocal microscope (FV10-ASW, Olympus, Japan). Fluorescence measurements were performed by simultaneous detection of green (484/510 nm) and red (581/591 nm) signals, and the green/red fluorescence ratio was used to quantify lipid peroxidation.

Total RNA was extracted by AG RNAex Pro Reagent (AG21101, Accurate Biology) and cDNA was synthesized using Evo M-MLV RT Premix (AG11706, Accurate Biology). Quantitative PCR was performed using the SYBR Green Premix SupTaqHS qPCR Kit (AG11718, Accurate Biology) with CFX Connect System (BioRad). The primer sequences used for determination of mRNA expression levels were as follows: ARNTL (BMAL1): Forward: CCAAGAAAGTATGGACACAGACAAA (5'-3'), Reverse: GCATTCTTGATCCTTCCTTGGT (5'-3'); β-actin: Forward: ACAGAGCCTCGCCTTTGCC (5'-3'), Reverse: GATATCATCATCCATGGTGAGCTGG (5'-3'). The relative fold change was calculated by the comparative CT method.

Cut&Tag Assay Kit was obtained from Novoprotein (China). Experiments were conducted using an anti-JUN antibody (Proteintech) following the manufacturer's instructions. Primer sequences used were listed below: PTGS2, Forward Primer: TGATCCACGCTCTTAGTTGAA (5'-3'), Reverse primer: AGGAAGCCTTTCTCCTCCTCT (5'-3').

Total RNA was extracted from HBE cells (cell line-based transcriptome sequencing) and mouse lung tissues using the TRIzol reagent following the manufacturer's protocols. The cDNA fragments were purified, end-repaired, poly(A)-tailed, and ligated to sequencing adapters. After PCR amplification and quality control, the libraries were sequenced on an Illumina platform. Cellular transcriptome sequencing was performed by Tsingke Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Tissue transcriptome sequencing was conducted by Novogene Bioinformatics Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China).

Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified with DESeq2 (|log2(fold change) | ≥ 1, Padj <0.05), and functional enrichment analysis (GO/KEGG) was performed using clusterProfiler (Version 4.6.2).

Mouse lung samples were collected and stored at −80 °C. Prior to liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis, the samples were thawed on ice, homogenized, and subjected to protein precipitation to remove interfering proteins. Non-targeted metabolomics analysis (HQ grade) was performed by Novogene Bioinformatics Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China), including metabolomic profiling via high-resolution LC-MS and subsequent bioinformatics analysis.

All the results analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (Version 9.0). Differences between the two groups were evaluated using an unpaired t -test or nonparametric tests. Differences across the three or more groups were analyzed by One-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons or nonparametric test. P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

title: Association between a four-locus gene model including IL13, IL4, FCER1B, and ADRB2 and asthma outcomes.
abstract: BackgroundThis study aimed to explore the association between a four-locus gene model and asthma outcomes.MethodsFour single-nucleotide polymorphisms were genotyped in 139 patients with different asthma outcomes (clinical remission, relapse, or persistence). The high-risk and low-risk genotypes for asthma were evaluated according to the different genotypes that they carried. Differences in asthma outcomes and the factors affecting asthma prognosis were analyzed.ResultsMore patients with high-risk genotypes had severe asthma attacks than those with low-risk genotypes. Compared with patients in asthma clinical remission, patients with severe asthma attacks were at risk for asthma relapse and asthma persistence. In addition, smoking was a risk factor for asthma persistence. The older the age of asthma onset, the more likely it was to be persistent. More patients in the high-risk genotype group had an age of asthma onset younger than 6 years old and an asthma course longer than 4 years than in the low-risk genotype group, regardless of the confounding factors.ConclusionsThe patients with high-risk genotypes not only had more severe asthma attacks and a younger age of asthma onset but also had a longer course, which suggested that the gene model could serve as a tool for asthma prognosis assessment with moderate utility.

sections.abstract:
This study aimed to explore the association between a four-locus gene model and asthma outcomes.

Four single-nucleotide polymorphisms were genotyped in 139 patients with different asthma outcomes (clinical remission, relapse, or persistence). The high-risk and low-risk genotypes for asthma were evaluated according to the different genotypes that they carried. Differences in asthma outcomes and the factors affecting asthma prognosis were analyzed.

More patients with high-risk genotypes had severe asthma attacks than those with low-risk genotypes. Compared with patients in asthma clinical remission, patients with severe asthma attacks were at risk for asthma relapse and asthma persistence. In addition, smoking was a risk factor for asthma persistence. The older the age of asthma onset, the more likely it was to be persistent. More patients in the high-risk genotype group had an age of asthma onset younger than 6 years old and an asthma course longer than 4 years than in the low-risk genotype group, regardless of the confounding factors.

The patients with high-risk genotypes not only had more severe asthma attacks and a younger age of asthma onset but also had a longer course, which suggested that the gene model could serve as a tool for asthma prognosis assessment with moderate utility.

Keywords: asthma, course, gene, model, outcome
sections.other:
In recent years, with the further understanding of and research on asthma, the prognosis and influencing factors of asthma have become the subjects of numerous studies. Asthma mostly occurs in preschool-aged children, and changes in airway structure and lung function damage resulting from asthma may begin earlier (). The wheezing phenotype in preschool-aged children can be divided into the following: (1) early transient wheezing: children whose wheezing disappears before 3 years old; (2) early onset persistent wheezing: children who develop the disease before the age of 3 generally experience wheezing symptoms that persist until school age, with some children still experiencing symptoms at the age of 12; and (3) delayed wheezing or asthma: children with typical characteristic backgrounds often experience asthma symptoms that persist into adulthood (). These different wheezing phenotypes suggest the necessity of paying attention to asthma outcomes. When children grow older, their immune function and body resistance improve, and some children with asthma experience symptom relief during puberty and adulthood. Studies have reported asthma relief rates ranging from 20% to 70% from childhood to adulthood (–).

Currently, there are few studies on childhood asthma outcomes. Prospective studies in multiple large birth cohorts have shown that the factors affecting the relief of childhood asthma are the following: (1) gender: asthma relief or self-healing mostly occurs in male patients, while being female is a risk factor for asthma lasting into adulthood (); (2) asthma severity: a follow-up birth cohort study found that childhood asthma severity determines prognosis and outcomes, and they proved that the more severe the childhood asthma is, the more likely it is to persist into adulthood (); (3) age of onset: there is controversy over the impact of onset age on the outcome of asthma. Some studies suggest that the younger the age of asthma onset, the greater the probability of recurrence and the more likely it is to persist into adulthood (). However, others indicate that the earlier the onset of asthma, the easier it is to alleviate it (); (4) manifestations: multiple sensitizations and early sensitization are risk factors for persistent childhood asthma; (5) combination of allergic diseases: most children with asthma have concurrent allergic diseases, such as allergic rhinitis and allergic dermatitis. Studies suggest that the accompanying allergic complications are risk factors for difficult-to-treat childhood asthma (); (6) airway hyper responsiveness: airway hyperresponsiveness and its severity are closely related to childhood asthma prognosis (); (7) mother’s allergy history: Dutch researchers followed up an asthma cohort for 39 years and found that a positive mother’s allergy history is one of the risk factors for childhood asthma to persist into adulthood (); and (8) genetics: some studies suggest that genetics can increase the risk of persistent asthma, and polygenic genetic risks can predict the occurrence and progression of childhood asthma (). There is limited understanding of which patients experience remission of asthma in adulthood and how it is related to genetic factors in China. Moreover, the natural course and treatment time of patients with asthma are also challenges faced by clinical doctors. Currently, there is no effective method to predict the course of patients with asthma. We suggest the hypothesis that a gene model can be used to predict the course of asthma in patients.

Hence, our study recruited patients with asthma of different onset ages and classified their asthma status based on their asthma development trend. The differences in asthma onset age and duration between different risk genotypes based on our model were compared. The aim was to elucidate the impact of genetic factors on the prognosis of childhood asthma in Han patients and provide a scientific basis for evaluating asthma prognosis.

sections.methods:
Our study recruited 139 patients with asthma from the Respiratory Clinic in Xinhua Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiaotong University School of Medicine. The study inclusion criteria consisted of the following: (1) adult patients diagnosed with bronchial asthma by doctors using the diagnostic criteria from the 2016 bronchial asthma prevention and treatment guidelines by the Asthma Group of the Respiratory Disease Branch of the Chinese Medical Association (); (2) individuals with a history of asthma but currently in remission; and (3) all participants were of Han ethnicity, aged 18–65, and had signed an informed consent. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) individuals with mental illness; (2) patients with asthma combined with consciousness disorders; and (3) patients with asthma combined with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. We collected asthma-related information from the included patients, including the age of asthma onset, current asthma status, clinical remission of asthma, recurrence and persistence of asthma after remission, severity of asthma attacks, personal allergy history, family history, and occupational risk factors. The study was approved by the ethics committee of the hospital (No. XHEC -D - 2016–393) and was conducted according to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

The genomic DNA of the four genes was extracted from the buccal mucosa using a DNA extraction kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The genotypes of the four gene loci were obtained using a multiplex polymerase chain reaction-restriction fragment length polymorphism assay (PCR-RFLP). The PCR cycling conditions were as follows: 95°C for 2 min; 45 cycles at 95°C for 30 s, 56°C for 30 s, and 72°C for 60 s; and finally, 72°C for 5 min. The conditions for the shrimp alkaline phosphatase (SAP) enzyme digestion reaction were 37°C for 40 min and then termination at 85°C for 5 min. The conditions used for iPLEX were 95°C for 30 s; 5 inner cycles at 52°C for 5 s and at 85°C for 5 s; and 40 outer cycles at 94°C for 5 s, 52°C for 5 s, and 85°C for 5 s. We then used matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry to discriminate between the four single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) ().

In our study, the different risk genotypes for asthma were discriminated according to the number of risk allele homozygotes. The control group comprised patients with no risk homozygotes (i.e., IL13 rs20541 AA or GA, IL4 rs2243250 CC or TC, ADRB2 rs1042713 GG or AG, and FCER1B rs569108 AA or AG). Those with different genotype combinations who had a significantly higher risk of asthma (if P < 0.05 and OR > 1) than the reference group were defined as being at higher genetic risk for asthma. The others were defined as being at lower genetic risk for asthma. The results for the different genotype combinations are shown in ().

In this study, the asthma status of patients was divided into clinical remission, recurrence after remission, or persistent asthma. Currently, there is no unified standard for the clinical remission of asthma. A study in Taiwan defined the absence of wheezing attacks in patients for 3 years prior to the follow-up cut-off as clinical remission of asthma (). In the study by Alberta et al., clinical remission of asthma was defined as simultaneously meeting the following three criteria: (a) no asthma symptom onset, (b) no use of anti-asthma drugs, and (c) no evidence of airflow restriction [lung function test: forced expiratory volume in 1 s/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) ≥ 80%], as of the year before the follow-up cutoff (). Complete remission of asthma requires a negative bronchial provocation test in addition to meeting the conditions for clinical remission. According to this standard, very few people will experience complete remission of asthma. In several studies, clinical remission was defined as the absence of asthma attacks in the 2 years prior to follow-up and at least 1 year without the use of anti-asthma drugs, resulting in reasonable results (, ). In addition, our previous studies on the outcome of wheezing in young children have also used the standard of no asthma symptoms in the 2 years prior to the follow-up cut-off point and no use of anti-asthma drugs for at least 1 year as clinical relief for wheezing (). Therefore, we will continue to use this method in our study. Asthma relapse after remission refers to the recurrence of asthma symptoms after at least 2 years of remission, or the use of asthma control drugs within the past year. Finally, persistent asthma refers to the absence of any asthma attacks for 2 years.

We used SPSS 20.0 (IBM, USA) to conduct the statistical analyses in this study. The quantitative data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Comparison of means between two samples was conducted using Student’s t -test or rank sum test, and Pearson χ 2 test or Fisher’s exact probability method was used to compare the differences in asthma status and duration between the patients with asthma with high-risk and low-risk genotypes. Logistic regression analysis was performed to elucidate the influencing factors for different asthma states in patients, and the odds ratio and 95% confidence interval were calculated. All the tests were double-sided tests, and the test level was α = 0.05, with P < 0.05 indicating a statistically significant difference.
sections.results:
In our study, 139 patients of the Han ethnicity were enrolled. The combinations of different asthma risk alleles carried by these patients were used to classify high- and low-risk asthma genotypes. The results showed that 62 patients had high-risk asthma genotypes and 77 had low-risk asthma genotypes. Women accounted for 53.23% of the high-risk genotype group, which was higher than that in the low-risk genotype group. There was no statistically significant difference between the two groups. In addition, 56.45% of the patients with high-risk genotypes experienced severe asthma attacks, which was higher than those with low-risk genotypes. This difference between the two groups was statistically significant. There were 36 patients with clinical remission of asthma, with a remission rate of 25.90%. Patients with recurrent and persistent asthma after remission accounted for 31.65% and 42.45%, respectively. There were no statistically significant differences in age, allergic rhinitis, eczema or atopic dermatitis, positive family allergy history, asthma history in first-degree relatives, smoking history, occupational risk factors, and different asthma states ().

We then used unordered multiclass logistic regression to analyze the factors affecting different asthma states in the patients. We found that compared with clinically relieved patients with asthma, severe asthma attacks are a risk factor for asthma recurrence and persistence after remission. The older the age of asthma onset, the more likely it was to be persistent, but it had no significant effect on asthma recurrence after remission. In addition, the patients with a positive smoking history were more likely to experience persistent asthma. Clinical remission of asthma was not significantly affected by gender, age, different asthma risk types, allergic rhinitis, eczema, family allergy history, asthma history in first-degree relatives, and occupational risk factors ().

We conducted a stratified analysis of the age of asthma onset and found that compared to patients with asthma with low-risk genotypes, more patients with asthma with high-risk genotypes developed symptoms before 6 years old. After adjusting for confounding factors such as gender and age, this result still showed statistical differences ().

We found that the average asthma course in the patients with high-risk genotypes was 19.43 years, while in the patients with low-risk genotypes, it was 14.21 years. While the former was higher than the latter, there was no significant statistical difference between the two groups. We further stratified the course of asthma and found that 79.03% of patients with asthma with high-risk genotypes had a course longer than 4 years, which was higher than the proportion of patients with asthma with a course ≤4 years. There was a statistically significant difference between the two groups, and after adjusting for confounding factors, such as gender and age, this result was still statistically significant ().
sections.discussion:
Asthma is an incurable chronic respiratory disease, and its outcome and prognosis remain challenges in scientific research. With research on complex asthma phenotypes, our understanding of asthma is no longer limited to controlling the condition, as uncovering the risk factors that affect the persistence or recurrence of asthma and intervening in the occurrence and development of asthma are particularly important. The development of asthma follows a certain natural trend, referred to as the “natural course” (). There are individual differences in the natural course of each patient, so it is difficult for doctors to determine how long each patient’s natural course is. The use of anti-asthma drugs can only control the condition of patients with asthma and cannot improve the natural course of the disease. The majority of asthma cases begin before school age, and some children may experience relief from asthma symptoms as they age and when their immune function changes. At present, research on asthma outcomes is mostly based on prospective follow-up studies in large birth cohorts. Due to the lack of a unified definition of asthma remission and persistence in these studies and the different follow-up times, reports on asthma remission rates vary. A study in a multiethnic population of patients with mild-to-moderate persistent childhood asthma showed a complete remission rate of 26% (). Research by Heldin et al. showed that approximately three-quarters of school-aged children experience asthma relief by mid-adulthood, which refers to the relief of clinical symptoms of asthma (). In addition, a follow-up study on asthma in children from birth to the age of 26 found that the wheezing relief rate in children was 27.4%, and wheezing symptoms persisted into adulthood in more than 1/4 of children (). In our study, the asthma clinical remission rate was 25.90% when using the criteria of no asthma symptoms in the 2 years prior to the follow-up cut-off point and no anti-asthma drugs used for at least 1 year.

This study identified the following three influencing factors affecting asthma outcomes: (1) asthma onset age, i.e., the older the age of asthma onset, the more likely it is for the patient to experience persistent asthma; (2) severity of asthma attacks, i.e., those who experience severe attacks are less likely to experience clinical remission; and (3) smoking history, i.e., a positive smoking history is a risk factor for persistent asthma. These findings are consistent with the results of multiple international studies on the prognostic factors of asthma. In addition, we also found that more patients with high-risk genotypes had more severe asthma attacks than those with low-risk genotypes, which indicates an association between the asthma susceptibility gene loci included in the gene model and severe asthma attacks (–). Severe asthma attacks are also a risk factor for asthma recurrence and persistence, so we speculate that the model can indirectly reflect these asthma outcomes. This study analyzed the onset age of patients with different asthma risk types and found that patients with asthma with high-risk genotypes had an earlier onset age. More than half of the patients with asthma with high-risk genotypes had already developed asthma before 6 years old, which is consistent with the fact that the majority of asthma cases occur in early childhood, especially preschool age. Furthermore, a subgroup analysis found that more patients with asthma with high-risk genotypes had a disease course of more than 4 years, indicating that the disease course of patients with asthma with high-risk genotypes is longer.

However, several study limitations should be acknowledged. First, the relatively small sample size in this study may have led to biased results. In addition, confounding factors were not adequately controlled, such as socioeconomic status, environmental exposures, adherence to medication, or access to healthcare. Therefore, subsequent studies should increase the sample size to enable more comprehensive analysis and further clarify the impact of this genetic model on asthma prognosis.

In summary, the study indicates that this four-locus gene model is related to the onset age, with patients with asthma with high-risk genotypes having an earlier onset age. In addition, compared with the patients with asthma with low-risk genotypes, the patients with asthma with high-risk genotypes had more severe asthma attacks and longer disease duration. Age of onset, severity of asthma, and smoking history are risk factors that affect asthma prognosis. These results fully demonstrate the association of the model with disease prognosis, providing strong evidence for clinical doctors to solve the treatment course problem in childhood asthma.

We found that the patients carrying high-risk genotypes exhibited more severe asthma attacks, an earlier age of onset, and a longer disease course. This research demonstrated that the model can be used to evaluate asthma prognosis to a certain extent.

title: Smoking asthma phenotype: diagnostic and management challenges.
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: The prevalence of active smoking in adults with asthma is similar to the general population. Smoking asthma is associated with poorer disease control, impaired response to corticosteroid therapy, accelerated decline in lung function, and increased rate of healthcare utilization. Current asthma guidelines do not provide specific treatment advice for smoking asthmatic patients. There is an urgent need for better understanding of the underlying mechanisms and effective treatment for smoking asthmatic patients. RECENT FINDINGS: An association between both active and passive smoking and adult-onset asthma is supported by many studies.The asthma-COPD overlap syndrome (ACOS) has recently gained particular interest and smoking asthmatic patients should be evaluated for ACOS.Treatment regimens for smoking asthma include higher doses of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), extrafine particle ICS formulations, antileukotrienes, and combinations of these options.Asthma is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular comorbidities whereas smoking is an additional strong independent risk factor for pulmonary and cardiovascular diseases. Tobacco smoking and not asthma per se seems to be the reason of poor prognosis, especially with regard to lung cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and mortality in asthmatic patients. SUMMARY: Smoking asthma represents a common challenge to the clinician both in terms of diagnosis and management. These aspects have not been thoroughly evaluated and deserve further investigation.

title: Efficacy Comparison of LPA2 Antagonist H2L5186303 and Agonist GRI977143 on Ovalbumin-Induced Allergic Asthma in BALB/c Mice.
abstract: Lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), an intercellular lipid mediator, is increased in the bronchoalveolar fluids of patients with asthma after allergen exposure. LPA administration exaggerates allergic responses, and the type 2 LPA receptor (LPA2) has been reported as a therapeutic target for asthma. However, results with LPA2 agonist and antagonist along with LPA2 gene deficient mice have been controversial and contradictory. We compared the effects of LPA2 antagonist (H2L5186303) and agonist (GRI977143) in a single experimental protocol of ovalbumin (OVA)-induced allergic asthma by treating drugs before antigen sensitization or challenge. H2L5186303 showed strong suppressive efficacy when administered before OVA sensitization and challenge, such as suppression of airway hyper responsiveness, inflammatory cytokine levels, mucin production, and eosinophil numbers. However, GRI977143 showed significant suppression when administered before an OVA challenge. Increases in eosinophil and lymphocyte counts in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, Th2 cytokine levels, inflammatory scores, and mucin production were differentially ameliorated by the two drugs. The results demonstrate the multiple roles of LPA2 in asthmatic responses. We suggest that the development of LPA2 antagonists would achieve better therapeutic efficacy against asthma than agonists.

sections.results:
Asthma is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by swollen and narrow airways []. Affected patients generally experience shortness of breath, chest tightness, coughing, and wheezing []. Pathological observations include eosinophil infiltration, mucus hyperproduction, and bronchial mucosal thickening and wall remodeling []. Asthmatic symptoms are usually controlled by corticosteroids, leukotriene D 4 antagonists, and long-acting β 2 adrenoceptor agonists []. However, drug-resistant asthma and steroid-induced side effects require novel approaches to overcome the limitations of such therapies [].

Lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) is a simple lipid mediator with variable acyl chain lengths. Studies suggest that LPA levels (22:5 and 22:6) are significantly increased in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) of asthmatic patients and mice challenged with segmental allergen and house dust mite (HDM), respectively [,,]. Additionally, LPA inhalation induces histamine release and enhances eosinophil and neutrophil infiltration into the lung alveolar spaces in guinea pigs [,]. Pro-inflammatory functions of LPA in immune cells have also been reported. According to a study, LPA induces calcium mobilization, actin reorganization, and chemotaxis in human eosinophils []. It also induces histamine release [] and chemokine generation via IL-4 in human mast cells []. Moreover, it also enhances IL-13 gene expression in Th2 cells in vitro [,]. In contrast, LPA attenuates cytokine secretion in human and murine dendritic cells [,]. LPA stimulates the expression of thymic stromal lymphopoietin and CCL20 [], and IL-8 production in primary cultured human bronchial epithelial cells by activating p38 MAP kinase and JNK [,]. In addition, the expression of LPA 2 was higher than LPA 1 in naïve T cells [], and in mouse tracheal epithelial cells LPA 2 mRNA showed the highest expression among LPA 1–4 []. Moreover, LPA 2 deficiency protects against bleomycin-induced lung injury and fibrosis [].

The involvement of LPA in allergic asthma and LPA 2 expression in epithelial and immune cells led to the investigation of the functional roles of LPA 2 in allergic asthma. Zhao et al. used a murine model of Schistosoma mansoni egg sensitization and challenged heterozygous LPA 2 gene deficient mice (LPA 2 +/− ). Results demonstrated a reduced influx of eosinophils and periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive cells in LPA 2 +/− compared to wild-type mice, suggesting a pro-inflammatory role of LPA 2 in allergic asthma development []. However, Emo et al. reported that OVA-sensitized and challenged homozygous LPA 2 gene-deficient mice (LPA 2 −/− ) showed more severe lung inflammation than wild-type mice, implying a negative regulation by LPA 2 signaling []. In contrast, attenuation of allergic lung inflammation and Th2 cytokines was observed in LPA 2 −/− mice challenged with three allergen (HDM, ragweed, and Aspergillus sp.) []. Previous studies suggest that LPA 2 antagonist H2L5186303 ((Z,Z)-4,4′-[1,3-phenylenebis(oxy-4,1-phenyleneimino)] bis [4-oxo-2-butenoic acid]) suppress allergic airway inflammation [,]. However, the LPA 2 agonist DBIBB (2-[4-(1,3-dioxo-1H,3H-benzoisoquinolin-2-yl)butylsulfamoyl] benzoic acid) also suppresses allergic eosinophilic bronchial inflammation []. Nevertheless, differences in asthma-inducing antigens, experimental protocols, and mouse genetic strains may lead to contradictory and controversial results. Therefore, we compared the effects of an LPA 2 antagonist (H2L5186303) and an LPA 2 agonist (GRI977143) on OVA-induced allergic asthma by providing drug treatment before antigen sensitization or challenge.

Antigen-induced cross-linking of the IgE-FcεRI complex activates mast cells and induces mast cell degranulation, which is the initial step in eliciting asthmatic response via release of histamine, leukotrienes, and neutral proteases. We measured the degranulation response in RBL-2H3 rat basophilic leukemia cells by assessing β-hexosaminidase activity after exposure to human serum albumin (antigen) (A). Results revealed that H2L5186303 treatment inhibited β-hexosaminidase release in a concentration-dependent manner (A), implying that LPA functions as a mast cell activator via LPA 2 . On the contrary, GRI977143 also inhibited inhibition of β-hexosaminidase release at 100 µM concentration, which was ten-fold higher than the effective concentration of H2L5186303 (10 µM) (A). This may imply a non-specific off-target effect of the LPA 2 agonist, GRI977143 (A).

In an OVA-induced mouse model of asthma, GRI977143 and H2L5186303 were intraperitoneally injected 30 min before OVA sensitization or challenge. As a result, an elevated total cell count in BALF was suppressed (A). The total cell count in BALF increased to 368.5% in the OVA-induced asthma compared to the PBS-treated control group (B); however, GRI977143 treatment before antigen challenge significantly suppressed the OVA-induced increase in total cell count by 75.5% (B). In addition, the immune cell population distribution was also assessed. Specifically, GRI977143 treatment before challenge significantly decreased the OVA-induced increase in eosinophil counts by 72.5% (B). Furthermore, H2L5186303 treatment before antigen sensitization and challenge significantly suppressed the OVA-induced increase in eosinophil counts by 60.9% and 63.7%, respectively. Moreover, an elevated lymphocyte count in response to OVA treatment was significantly decreased by 73.4% and 70.7% by GRI977143 treatment before challenge and H2L5186303 treatment before sensitization, respectively (C). However, macrophage count was not significantly increased by OVA treatment.

The effects of GRI977143 and H2L5186303 on AHR were measured. Results showed that the Penh value of the OVA-challenged mice was higher than the control group. A significantly reduced AHR was observed in OVA-challenged mice treated with GRI977143 before OVA challenge but not sensitization (). Moreover, H2L5186303 treatment before OVA sensitization and challenge significantly reduced AHR in OVA-challenged mice ().

Histological studies using H&E and PAS staining of lung samples showed an increased inflammation and mucin secretion. Eosinophils were observed as small, dark blue dots in H&E staining of the lung sections (A). There were few eosinophils in the PBS control compared with those observed around the bronchioles in the OVA group (A). GRI977143 before OVA challenge and H2L5186303 before OVA sensitization or challenge inhibited OVA-induced elevated eosinophil counts (A). Semi-quantitative evaluation of lung inflammation (using a scale of 0–3) indicated an average inflammation score of 2.168 in the OVA-treated group, which was significantly reduced after GRI977143 and H2L5186303 treatments before the challenge (C).

Mucin and mucous glycoproteins produced by goblet cells were visualized by PAS staining of the lung sections. Mucin-secreting cells were observed as dark violet spots surrounding bronchioles in the OVA group (B). PAS staining was inhibited after GRI977143 treatment before the OVA challenge and H2L5186303 treatment before OVA sensitization or challenge (B). Furthermore, mucin production was estimated by counting the number of PAS-positive cells in the bronchioles (D). Results demonstrated that stained cells were scarce in the PBS-treated group; however, approximately 100 PAS-positive cells/mm were detected in the OVA-treated group, which were significantly reduced after GRI977143 and H2L5186303 treatments before the OVA challenge (D).

Th2 cells contribute to the pathogenesis of allergic asthma by producing Th2 cytokines, such as IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, leading to eosinophil accumulation in the airway wall, mucus overproduction, and IgE synthesis. In addition, Th1 and Th17 cytokines are involved in late-stage pathogenesis of asthma. Therefore, changes in the mRNA levels of the Th2 cytokines IL-4 and IL-13, and Th1 cytokine IFN-γ were measured by qPCR in BALF cells. As shown in , the mRNA levels of all three cytokines were increased in the BALF cells of the OVA group; however, H2L5186303 treatment before OVA sensitization or challenge significantly suppressed the elevated IL-4 and IL-13 levels (). In addition, GRI977143 treatment before OVA sensitization or challenge suppressed the cytokine levels but to a non-significant level (). This was consistent with the findings of mild suppression of BALF total cell count, lung inflammation, and mucin production after GRI977143 and H2L5186303 treatments before OVA sensitization or challenge.

Furthermore, changes in the mRNA levels of Th2 and Th1 cytokines in the lungs were measured using qPCR. As shown in , the mRNA levels of the five cytokines increased in the lungs of the OVA group, and GRI977143 treatment before OVA challenge significantly suppressed the elevated IL-4, IL-5, and IL-33 levels (). However, H2L5186303 treatment before OVA sensitization did not significantly suppress the OVA-induced increase ().

Th2 cytokines, such as IL-13 play a major role in the progression of allergic asthma. Th2 cytokines induce eosinophil recruitment and activation, mucus hypersecretion in epithelial cells, metaplasia of goblet cells, and the proliferation of smooth muscle cells. Protein levels of the Th2 cytokine IL-13 in the BALF were measured by ELISA, and results showed elevated IL-13 levels in the OVA-induced compared with those in the PBS-treated control group. Moreover, the elevated IL-13 levels were suppressed by GRI977143 and H2L5186303 treatments (A). Furthermore, serum IgE levels were assessed to confirm the immunological effects induced by OVA, GRI977143, and H2L5186303 treatments. Results revealed that IgE levels were increased in the sera of OVA-treated mice (B); however, these elevated levels were not suppressed by GRI977143 or H2L5186303 treatments before antigen sensitization and challenge.

Previous findings have suggested various pro-allergic and pro-inflammatory responses of LPA as follows: (1) LPA inhalation induces histamine release and enhances eosinophil infiltration into alveolar spaces in guinea pigs [,]; (2) LPA not only induces chemotaxis of human eosinophils and chemokine generation through IL-4 in human mast cells but also enhances IL-13 gene expression in Th2 cells in vitro [,,,]; (3) LPA stimulated the expression of thymic stromal lymphopoietin and CCL20 in bronchial epithelial cells []; and (4) The LPA levels of C22:5 and C22:6 increased in the BALF of asthmatic patients and mice after allergen challenge [,,]. Additionally, the pro-allergic roles of LPA were experimentally linked to LPA 2 by three studies. Two studies showed a reduction in eosinophil influx and attenuation of Th2 cytokines in LPA 2 gene-deficient mice (LPA 2 +/− and LPA 2 −/− ) [,], whereas a third study showed that H2L5186303 suppresses allergic airway inflammation []. Our results with the LPA 2 antagonist H2L5186303 also support the pro-allergic responses of LPA and the role of LPA 2 . Kondo et al. showed that H2L5186303 improved AHR and reduced eosinophil infiltration and PAS-positive cell counts, suggesting that LPA 2 -mediated increase in CCL2 leads to macrophage activation and IL-33 production in allergic responses in the lung []. In the present study, we reproduced the previous findings of AHR improvement, eosinophil infiltration reduction, and suppression of mucin secretion. In addition, we reported two novel findings: (1) H2L5186303 suppressed mast cell degranulation, and (2) H2L5186303 was effective not only when delivered before antigen challenge but also before sensitization.

In contrast, several findings indicated LPA-mediated anti-allergic responses as follows: (1) LPA induced IL-13Rα2 (IL-13 decoy receptor) expression and release, and attenuated IL-13-induced phosphorylation of STAT6 in human bronchial epithelial cells []; (2) LPA attenuated cytokine secretion in human and murine dendritic cells [,]; (3) LPA 2 gene-deficient mice (LPA 2 −/− ) showed more lung inflammation than wild-type mice []; and (4) LPA 2 agonist DBIBB suppressed allergic bronchial inflammation []. Emo et al. observed more severe allergen-driven lung inflammation in LPA 2 −/− than in wild-type mice in allergic asthma models of both systemic and mucosal sensitization, in contrast to the above-mentioned experiments using LPA 2 −/− mice [,,]. Such discrepancies may result from difference in the origin of LPA 2 −/− mice, i.e., Dr Chun’s lab vs. Deltagen, and their different adaptations to LPA 2 gene deficiency. In addition, the experimental protocol used by Emo et al. was also different, where allergen-pulsed LPA 2 −/− dendritic cells were adoptively transferred to wild-type mice owing to their hyperactivity in vitro []. This observation is consistent with the finding that LPA attenuates cytokine secretion in human and murine dendritic cells [,]. Consequently, LPA 2 deficiency leads to cytokine hyper secretion due to a lack of LPA 2 negative regulation. In this context, the results obtained with the LPA 2 agonist DBIBB were consistent [] in which HDM extract was delivered intranasally for 10 consecutive days and DBIBB was administered intraperitoneally []. Therefore, DBIBB was delivered during the antigen sensitization period, which suppressed the activation of dendritic cells. However, negative regulation via LPA 2 was partly seen in our results with GRI977143. We observed significant AHR improvement, reduced eosinophils infiltration, and suppressed mucin secretion only with GRI977143 treatment before antigen challenge but not before sensitization, which is in contrast to previous observations of LPA 2 negative regulation of dendritic cell activation. One intriguing point is that DBIBB can inhibit autotaxin activity, which produces LPA from lysophosphatidylcholine, implying that DBIBB not only activates LPA 2 but also inhibits LPA production in the lung []. This may compound the results, as inhibition of LPA production could result in similar results as LPA 2 antagonism. It seems that the LPA 2 antagonist H2L5186303 did not inhibit autotaxin activity, as LPA levels in BALF were not affected by H2L5186303 [].

Contradictory and contrasting results on LPA 2 functions in allergic asthma models have been observed. We compared the results with the LPA 2 agonist and antagonist in a single experimental protocol to gain a clear conclusion. Our findings revealed that the LPA 2 antagonist H2L5186303 effectively suppresses the symptoms and immunologic responses in treatments before antigen sensitization and challenge. This supports the pro-allergic roles of LPA 2 in allergic inflammation [,,]. We also observed that the LPA 2 agonist GRI977143 was effective in suppressing allergic responses only in treatment before antigen challenge, unlike the previously known negative regulation of dendritic cell activation by LPA 2 [,]. The differences may result from the nature of allergens, such as HDM and OVA, the methods of sensitization and challenge, such as mucosal and systemic, the genetic backgrounds of the mice, such as C57BL/6 and BALB/c, and the timing of administration, such as before sensitization and challenge. In addition to the above-mentioned immune cells, bronchial epithelial cells and airway smooth muscle cells are also involved in allergic asthma reactions [,,,], which makes the interpretation of the results at the level of target cells and molecular mechanisms difficult. In addition, there are differences in LPA 2 expression between mice and humans [].

Conclusively, the present results demonstrate multiple roles of LPA 2 in asthmatic responses and suggest that the development of LPA 2 antagonists would achieve better therapeutic efficacy against asthma than agonists, although it would be a challenge to develop a therapeutic targeting LPA 2 . However, local delivery might be an option to reduce systemic side effects.

H2L5186303, GRI977143, OVA, and alum were procured from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA).

Rat RBL-2H3 mast cells were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA) and cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle medium (DMEM)-high glucose containing 10% ( v / v ) heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum along with 2 mM glutamine, 100 U/mL penicillin, 1 mM sodium pyruvate, and 50 μg/mL streptomycin at 37 °C in a 5% CO 2 -humidified incubator.

Five-week-old female BALB/c mice were purchased from Daehan Biolink (Seoul, Korea) and maintained in the laboratory animal facility at Kyung Hee University by providing water and food ad libitum . The Institutional Animal Care Committee of the university reviewed and approved the study protocol, considering the ethical principles and the care and use of animals for scientific purposes (Approval Number, KHSASP-21-352).

Degranulation of RBL-2H3 cells was assessed by measuring β-hexosaminidase activity in the medium. Mouse monoclonal anti-dinitrophenyl immunoglobulin E (DNP-IgE) and human DNP albumin were used to induce degranulation [].

Following a simple randomization procedure, six-week-old female BALB/c mice (approximately 22 g) were randomly assigned to six treatment groups ( n = 5): PBS-injected control group, OVA-injected asthma group, GRI977143 (1 mg/kg) treatment before sensitization plus OVA-injected group, GRI977143 treatment before challenge plus OVA-injected group, H2L5186303 (1 mg/kg) treatment before sensitization plus OVA-injected group, and H2L5186303 treatment before challenge plus OVA-injected group. Asthma was induced by intraperitoneal injection of 50 μg OVA and 1 mg aluminum hydroxide on days 0 (D0) and 14 (D14; sensitization). The mice were challenged with nebulized OVA on D28, D29, and D30 (challenge). GRI977143 or H2L5186303 was administered via intraperitoneal injection 30 min before OVA sensitization or challenge. BALF was collected from the lung tissues on D32 followed by staining for cell population analysis [].

Immune cells in BALF were adhered to a glass slide using a Cellspin ® centrifuge (Hanil Electric, Seoul, Republic of Korea) and fixed in methanol for 30 s. Cells were stained with May–Grünwald solution for 8 min, followed by Giemsa solution for 12 min.

Lung sections from mice in each group were prepared and examined. Briefly, left lungs were fixed in 10% formalin and dehydrate 30% sucrose solution and embedded in O.C.T. compound. Sections (7 µm) were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), and periodic acid-Schiff (PAS; using Schiff’s reagent) stain to identify eosinophil infiltration and mucus-secreting cells (goblet cells) in the airways, respectively. The right lung tissue was crushed, put in 1 mL of trizol, stored, extracted and synthesized and then confirmed by qPCR.

The degree of lung inflammation was estimated by a treatment-blinded observer using a subjective scale of 0–3. PAS-stained mucin-secreting cells in the airways were counted in two lung sections per mouse. Consequently, mucous production was expressed as the number of PAS-positive cells per millimeter of bronchiole. Moreover, the length of the bronchial basal lamina was measured using ImageJ software (National Institute of Health).

Airway hyper-responsiveness (AHR) was detected using noninvasive whole-body plethysmography (Model PLY-UNR-MS2; EMKA Technologies, Paris, France) 24 h after the last OVA treatment.

Mouse serum IgE and IL-13 levels were determined using ELISA kits (eBioscience, San Diego, CA, USA). IL-13 specific capture and biotinylated antibodies were obtained from eBioscience (IL-4: Cat. No. 14-7041-68 and 33-7042-68C, IL-13: Cat no. 14-7043-68 and 33-7135-68B; San Diego, CA, USA). Avidin-horseradish peroxidase was used, and the absorbance was measured at 450 nm.

Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software, Inc., La Jolla, CA, USA). Data were expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s multiple comparison test was used to compare the differences among multiple groups. Differences were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05.

The Institutional Animal Care Committee of the Kyung Hee University reviewed and approved the study protocol, considering the ethical principles and the care and use of animals for scientific purposes (Approval Number, KHSASP-21-352).
