sections.methods:
The UKB was a large population-based prospective cohort study of more than 500,000 adults aged 37–73 years in England, Scotland, and Wales between 2006 and 2010 []. The theoretical basis and design of the study are detailed in []. Participants attended 22 assessment centers in England, Scotland, and Wales, completing a touchscreen questionnaire, a short computer-assisted interview, and physical measurements. Blood, urine, and saliva samples were collected from all participants at baseline using strict quality control. The study was based on UKB data that had been approved by the North West Multi-Center Research Ethics Committee, and all participants signed a written informed consent form [].

Study population included in this study were those with asthma, self-reported history of asthma according to the baseline questionnaire or International Classification of Diseases codes − 10 (ICD-10 codes: J45, J46). The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) participants without electronic medical records and self-reported disease data ( n = 10,957); (2) participants with prevalent CVD at baseline ( n = 174,155); and (3) those with missing serum 25(OH)D measurements ( n = 17,954). After these exclusions, a total of 281,783 participants were included in the final cohort, comprising 30,534 patients with asthma and 251,249 non-asthma controls (Figure E1).

The biomarker measurements are described in detail in the online UKB Showcase ( https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/ ). Serum 25(OH)D levels (nmol/L) at baseline were measured using chemiluminescent immunoassay on the Sorin Group Liaison XL platform. The analytical range of this method was 10–375 nmol/L. The coefficients of variation for the low, medium, and high internal quality control samples of 25(OH)D were 6.14%, 5.39% and 5.04%, respectively, and the results of the external quality control were 100% [].

The rs1544410 ( BsmI ), rs2228570 ( FokI ), rs731236 ( TaqI ), and rs7975232 ( ApaI ) polymorphisms are among the most representative and functional single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the VDR gene []. Owing to their marked functional relevance, these SNPs have been extensively investigated. Given their significant functional implications, we further evaluated whether these loci modulate the association between vitamin D status and CVD risk.

The primary outcome of interest was the CVD incidence. The occurrence and timing information of CVD in the study population was based on admission data from Episode Statistics-Admitted Patient Care (England), Scottish Morbidity Records-General/ Acute Inpatient and Day Case Admissions (Scotland), and Patient Episode Database for Wales until 31 Sep 2022. The diagnosis of CVD was confirmed through codes as ICD-9, ICD-10, and Operative Procedures Coding System-4 (OPCS-4) (Table E1).

The baseline covariates include self-reported demographic information, socio-economic status, lifestyle, and other factors. (i) demographic factors: age, sex, race and ethnicity; (ii) socio-economic factors: Townsend Deprivation Index (higher values indicate higher levels of material deprivation), education, employment; (iii) lifestyle factors: smoking status, frequency of alcohol intake, physical activity (as measured by the short International Physical Activity Questionnaire []), healthy diet (we used the following items (meeting 2 or more) to define a healthy diet: total fruit and vegetable intake > 4.5 pieces/day, total fish intake > 2 times/week, processed meat intake ≤ 2 times/week and red meat intake ≤ 5 times/week []); (iv) Other: the season of blood collection (spring: March-May, summer: June-August, autumn: September-November, winter: December-February), body mass index (BMI, kg/m 2 ).

To quantify the extent to which specific biological pathways explain the association between serum 25(OH)D and incident CVD in asthma patients, we performed a formal causal mediation analysis. This analysis allows for the decomposition of the total effect of 25(OH)D on CVD risk into a direct effect (path independent of the mediators) and an indirect effect (path operating through the specified mediators). We selected BMI, C-reactive protein (CRP), and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) as potential mediators based on strong a priori biological rationale. These variables represent the key interconnected pathways of adiposity, systemic inflammation, and glucose metabolism, respectively, all of which are influenced by 25(OH)D and are established contributors to cardiovascular pathogenesis.

According to the Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guidelines, vitamin D status was classified into 4 groups based on baseline serum 25 (OH)D levels: severe vitamin D deficiency (< 25.0 nmol/L), moderate vitamin D deficiency (25.0-49.9 nmol/L), vitamin D insufficiency (50.0-74.9 nmol/L), and vitamin D sufficiency (≥ 75.0 nmol/L) []. The person-years of each participant were calculated from the date of recruitment until the date of reported disease diagnosis, death, or loss to follow-up, whichever occured first. Continuous variables in the baseline characteristics were reported as mean (standard deviation, SD) or median (Quartile1, Quartile3) and categorical variables were reported as N (%).

The restricted cubic spline (RCS) model was used to explore the dose–response associations of baseline serum 25(OH)D levels and the risk of outcome events after adjusting for confounding variables. We chose the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of 25(OH)D levels as the nodes to fit the best approximation model, and the lowest value of serum 25(OH)D concentration as the reference point and tested for linearity using the Wald test.

Cox proportional regression models were constructed to calculate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the association between serum 25(OH)D levels and the risk of incident endpoint events. Model 1 was adjusted for sex (female/male), age (continuous); Model 2 was further adjusted for race and ethnicity (White/non-White), education (no qualification/secondary education/vocational qualification/higher education), healthy diet (yes/no), smoking status (never/former/current), frequency of alcohol intake (daily/monthly to weekly/never or special occasions); Model 3 was further adjusted for the season of blood collection (spring/summer/autumn/winter). These three models were analyzed in asthma groups. The serum 25(OH)D concentration was analyzed as a continuous variable after natural logarithmic transformation.

The interaction between serum 25(OH)D levels and VDR genetic variants was evaluated by including a multiplicative interaction term in the Cox proportional hazards model, and its significance was tested using the Wald test. We further conducted a stratified analysis to evaluate the combined effects of serum 25(OH)D levels and VDR genetic variants on CVD risk.

To quantify the underlying biological pathways, a formal mediation analysis was performed using the Bootstrap method with 1,000 resamples to estimate the extent to which log-transformed CRP (Not meeting the normal distribution), BMI, and HbA1c mediated the association between vitamin D and CVD risk. In parallel, to contextualize the risk specific to asthma, we employed Cox proportional hazards models to compare the incidence of CVD across different 25(OH)D categories, directly contrasting asthmatic participants with their non-asthmatic counterparts.

To verify the robustness of the results, we performed further series of subgroup and sensitivity analyses. First, stratified analyses were performed according to age (< 60 years/ ≥ 60 years), sex (female/ male), education (no qualification/secondary education/vocational qualification/higher education), and BMI (< 30 kg/m 2 / ≥ 30 kg/m 2 ). Within each subgroup, the association between serum 25(OH)D levels and outcome events was assessed separately (using Cox regression analysis as before), and the results were compared between subgroups to assess whether there were significant differences. Second, we performed a series of sensitivity analyses to (i) exclude individuals who had an outcome event early in the follow-up period (within 2 year) to reduce the effect of potential reverse causality, (ii) limit the population to the Whites; (iii) analysis of the mediating role of non-natural logarithmic transformation of CRP and (iv) make additional adjustments to lifestyle factors: sleep duration and physical activity.

Our study used R (4.4.3) for all analyses, and a two-sided P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For multiple comparisons, the Bonferroni correction threshold was used to define statistical significance.
sections.results:
A total of 30,534 participants with asthma were included in the final analysis after applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Among them, 17,807 were female (58.3%) and 12,727 were male (41.7%), with an mean age of 54.1 (8.3) years.

The mean serum 25(OH)D level in all subjects was 47.1 (19.6) nmol/L. 17,421 (57.1%) participants had moderate and severe vitamin D deficiency. Higher levels of 25(OH)D concentrations were more commonly observed in participants who were White, had a lower BMI, consumed alcohol frequently, had never smoked, reported longer sleep duration, engaged in moderate-to-high physical activity, and had blood samples collected in summer (Table , Page 33–37).

Restricted cubic spline analysis revealed a significant non-linear L-shaped association between 25(OH)D concentration and the risk of CVD incidence in patients with asthma ( P non−linear = 0.002) after full adjustment (Model 3). The adjusted HRs indicated a strong inverse association at lower 25(OH)D levels, which tended to stabilize at approximately 50 nmol/L (Fig. ).

During a median follow-up of 14.8 (9.9, 15.8) years, a total of 9857 (32.3%) sudden CVD events occurred among patients with asthma. Across all multivariable-adjusted Cox regression models, a significant inverse association was consistently observed between 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk in patients with asthma. In Model 3, using the group with 25(OH)D levels < 25.0 nmol/L as the reference, the HRs for CVD risk in the higher 25(OH)D categories were as follows: 0.90 (95% CI: 0.85–0.96) for 25.0-49.9 nmol/L, 0.83 (95% CI: 0.78–0.89) for 50.0-74.9 nmol/L, and 0.83 (95% CI: 0.76–0.91) for ≥ 75.0 nmol/L ( P for trend < 0.001). Notably, the identical HRs and substantial overlap in CIs between the 50.0-74.9 nmol/L and ≥ 75.0 nmol/L groups indicated that the CVD risk reduction stabilizes, implying a threshold effect around 50 nmol/L (Table , Page 38). In addition, per each 1-unit increment in log-transformed 25(OH)D levels was associated with 14% (95% CI: 18 − 10%, P < 0.001) decreased risks of CVD.

Genetic analysis revealed that the FokI (rs2228570) G allele was modestly but significantly associated with increased serum 25(OH)D levels ( P = 0.012), whereas the other three SNPs ( BsmI , TaqI , and ApaI ) showed no significant associations with 25(OH)D status (Table E2). Moreover, no significant associations were observed between VDR genetic variants and CVD risk (all P for trend > 0.05) (Table E3).

In multivariable-adjusted models, the relationship between 25(OH)D and CVD was not modified by VDR genetic variants, under either additive, dominant, or recessive genetic models (all P interaction > 0.05) (Table , Page 39). However, in stratified analyses by 25(OH)D levels, significant associations were observed in the severe deficiency group. In this deficient group, the BsmI (rs1544410) T allele was associated with an increased risk of CVD (HR = 1.09, 95% CI 1.01–1.17, P = 0.025). A similar trend was observed for the FokI (rs2228570) G allele (HR = 1.08, 95% CI 1.00-1.16, P = 0.050). In contrast, the ApaI (rs7975232) A allele exhibited a protective effect (HR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.86–0.99, P = 0.036). These associations were absent in participants with other 25(OH)D groups (≥ 25.0 nmol/L) (Fig. ).

Further analysis specifically testing for interaction effects within the severe vitamin D deficient asthmatic subgroup revealed significant modification effects. We found that the BsmI (rs1544410) T allele and TaqI (rs731236) G allele significantly attenuated the protective effect of vitamin D, showing significant interactions under both additive ( P interaction = 0.025 and 0.050, respectively) and recessive models ( P interaction = 0.045 and 0.020, respectively). Conversely, the ApaI (rs7975232) A allele significantly enhanced vitamin D’s protective effect, demonstrating significant interactions under both additive ( P interaction = 0.036) and dominant models ( P interaction = 0.014) (Table , Page 40). These findings indicate that severe vitamin D deficiency significantly modifies the relationship between VDR genetic variants and CVD risk in the asthma patients.

Mediation analysis identified BMI, systemic inflammation (log_CRP), and glycemic control (HbA1c) as significant mediators. BMI accounted for the largest proportion (35.5%) of the association, followed by log_CRP (20.7%) and HbA1c (9.9%). The indirect effects for all three mediators were statistically significant (Table , Page 41).

Serum 25(OH)D levels were inversely associated with CVD risk among patients with asthma, with a more pronounced increase in risk observed at lower concentrations. Compared to the non-asthma group, asthma patients with 25(OH)D levels < 25.0 nmol/L had the highest risk (HR = 1.27, 95% CI: 1.21–1.34). This risk gradually decreased with higher vitamin D categories but remained significant even at levels ≥ 75.0 nmol/L (HR = 1.07, 95% CI: 1.00-1.14) (Table , Page 42). All associations were statistically significant ( P < 0.05).

The association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk remained stable across subgroups defined by age, sex, employment, and BMI (Table E4). In the sensitivity analysis, to minimize the possibility of reverse causation, we excluded participants who developed CVD within the first two years of follow-up. The results obtained from this analysis were consistent with the primary findings. (Table E5). The association remained consistent when the analysis was restricted to White participants (Table E6), suggesting that the observed relationship was not solely driven by ethnic differences in vitamin D status. The sensitivity analysis with un-natural transformed CRP revealed a significant but substantially weaker mediation effect (7.6%), confirming that log-transformation is necessary to fully capture the role of systemic inflammation (Table E7). Furthermore, further adjustment for potential confounding, including sleep duration and physical activity, did not alter the effect estimates (Table E8).
sections.discussion:
Our study was a large-scale prospective cohort analysis of 281,783 individuals from the UKB, comprising 30,534 patients with asthma and 251,249 non-asthma controls, with a follow-up period of approximately 15 years. We found that serum 25(OH)D levels were significantly and non-linearly associated with the risk of CVD in the population with asthma. The CVD risk decreased progressively with higher 25(OH)D levels but plateaued at approximately 50 nmol/L. Furthermore, mediation analysis revealed that BMI, systemic inflammation (log-CRP), and HbA1c significantly mediated this association. Compared to non-asthma controls, asthma patients with severe vitamin D deficiency had the highest CVD risk, which remained significant even at sufficient levels. In asthma patients with severe vitamin D deficiency, our analysis revealed that VDR genetic variants (rs1544410, rs731236, rs7975232) exerted significant modifying effects on the protective association of 25(OH)D against CVD. These findings were consistent across multiple subgroup and sensitivity analyses, underscoring the robustness of our results and highlighting vitamin D as a potentially modifiable factor for CVD prevention in patients with asthma.

Multiple clinical studies have indicated that low serum 25(OH)D levels are associated with an increased risk of CVD in healthy people or those with certain diseases [–]. For example, a large cohort study of British adults reported a non-linear association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk, showing a threshold effect at approximately 35 nmol/L, below which the risk of CVD increased significantly []. Also, Mendelian randomization studies have provided evidence that vitamin D deficiency increases the risk of CVD [, ]. In patients with vitamin D deficiency (< 50 nmol/L), randomized controlled trials (RCT) have demonstrated that high-dose vitamin D supplementation confered significant cardiovascular benefits, including reduced aortic systolic blood pressure, vascular stiffness, and arterial wave reflection in general cohorts [], as well as improved left ventricular ejection fraction and ventricular remodeling indices in those with chronic heart failure []. Whether vitamin D deficiency contributes to CVD risk in asthma patients has remained unclear. Our study provides new evidence addressing this gap, demonstrating a significant, non-linear inverse association between serum 25(OH)D and CVD risk specifically in asthma patients.

By contrast, some studies in the general population have reported null associations. An observational study of 1,798 elderly people in Asia showed that serum 25(OH)D concentration was not significantly associated with the risk of subclinical atherosclerosis []. Similarly, an RCT of 5108 community members with an mean age of 66 years showed no significant effect of vitamin D supplementation on cardiovascular health []. A plausible explanation for these inconsistencies lies in differences among the study populations. Most null findings have come from trials in the general population, many of whom had sufficient 25(OH)D levels at baseline. In our study, we identified a threshold effect, with CVD risk declining as serum 25(OH)D increased but plateauing at around 50 nmol/L. Trials that predominantly enrolled individuals above this threshold may therefore have underestimated or failed to detect the benefits of supplementation.

Moreover, current related studies have several limitations. For example, the study populations were mostly single-center, small-scale, and short-term, and the data on vitamin D intake in the diet and the sun exposure time of patients may not be considered []. In addition, existing RCTs have focused on the effect of vitamin D supplementation on the severity of disease and the risk of developing asthma in the offspring of patients with allergic diseases [–]. There is limited evidence regarding whether vitamin D interventions in patients with asthma have a protective effect on incident CVD. Our findings suggest a clear inverse association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk in asthma patients. This conclusion provides us with a future research direction; that is, it is necessary to carry out large-scale, multi-center, long-term follow-up RCTs on asthma patients to gain a deeper understanding of the impact of vitamin D supplementation on subsequent CVD risk.

In addition to serum 25(OH)D levels, we further examined the potential impact of VDR genetic variants. Of the four SNPs we examined, rs2228570 ( FokI ) alters the translation initiation site, producing VDR isoforms of different lengths []. The GG genotype of rs2228570 ( FokI ) encodes the shorter isoform with reduced transcriptional activity [], which may trigger compensatory synthesis of 25(OH)D to maintain calcium-phosphorus homeostasis []. Such a putative negative feedback mechanism could explain our results, finding that the GG genotype of rs2228570 ( FokI ) is associated with higher serum 25(OH)D levels. Bioinformatics analysis suggested that the intron variants rs1544410 ( BsmI ) and rs7975232 ( ApaI ), and the synonymous variant rs731236 ( TaqI ), may modulate VDR function by altering DNA secondary structure and mRNA splicing, thereby affecting its transcriptional regulation []. Our study demonstrates that the VDR gene polymorphism ( BsmI , TaqI , ApaI ) significantly modifies the protective effect of 25(OH)D on the onset of CVD in asthma patients with severe vitamin D deficiency. Consistent with this, an UKB clinical study revealed that the T allele of the rs1544410 ( BsmI ) polymorphism attenuates the protective effect of vitamin D against cardiometabolic multimorbidity []. This result highlights the importance of considering an individual’s genetic background of VDR simultaneously when assessing the impact of vitamin D on cardiovascular health and provides potential targets for precise prevention.

Potential mechanisms may underlie the inverse correlation between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk in patients with asthma. First, vitamin D deficiency contributes to immune dysregulation, suppressing regulatory T cell differentiation while promoting Th1 and Th17 responses. This shift enhances the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β) and reduces anti-inflammatory mediators (e.g., IL-10, IL-4), thereby amplifying cardiovascular inflammation [–]. Second, 1,25(OH) 2 D 3 also modulates the renin–angiotensin system (RAS), a central pathway in cardiovascular regulation []. Through the VDR, 1,25(OH) 2 D 3 inhibits renin gene expression and reduces angiotensin II production [], and down-regulates the expression of angiotensin II type 1 receptor, thereby limiting the production of reactive oxygen species and improving endothelial cell (ECs) function []. When vitamin D is deficient, this inhibitory control is lost, may lead to over-activation of the RAS, exacerbating oxidative stress, myocardial damage, and vasoconstriction, and causing hypertension and cardiac hypertrophy. Third, vitamin D deficiency may also impair vascular homeostasis. In endothelial cells, it increases NF-κB and IL-6 expression, thereby reducing vasodilatory function []. At the same time, it suppresses the proliferation and migration of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), compromising vascular repair []. Therefore, vitamin D deficiency may affect vascular health and the development of CVD by causing impaired functions of ECs and VSMCs. In addition to the above, further studies are needed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the potential protective effect of vitamin D against CVD in patients with asthma.

Our mediation analysis indicates that the inverse association between serum 25(OH)D and CVD risk in patients with asthma is partially explained by lower body mass index (BMI), reduced systemic inflammation (CRP), and better glycemic control (HbA1c). This finding supports the hypothesis that vitamin D may confer cardiovascular protection in this population by mitigating key cardiometabolic risk pathways. The biological plausibility of these mediating pathways is well-established: (1) Adiposity (BMI): Vitamin D acts directly on fat cells in its active form, 1,25(OH) 2 D, which can improve their glucose metabolism, promote fat breakdown, and exert a powerful anti-inflammatory effect, thereby helping to maintain the normal function of fat cells and delay aging []. Moreover, there is clinical evidence suggesting that vitamin D deficiency is associated with unhealthy obesity patterns and ectopic fat deposition []. (2) Inflammation (CRP): Vitamin D has potent anti-inflammatory properties. It can exert anti-inflammatory effects by down-regulating the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-17 and IL-6 []. Research evidence from the Mendelian randomization method indicates an L-shaped causal association between low levels of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D and higher levels of C-reactive protein []. (3) Glucose Metabolism (HbA1c): Vitamin D can improve insulin resistance by reducing pro-inflammatory factors and enhancing the function of insulin receptors []. Moreover, clinical studies have confirmed that the level of vitamin D is negatively correlated with the degree of insulin resistance, and supplementing vitamin D can effectively reduce the risk of insulin resistance [, ]. In asthma, a condition frequently associated with underlying metabolic dysregulation and chronic inflammation, vitamin D deficiency could act as a key exacerbating factor. It may potentiate the vicious cycle linking obesity, inflammation, and insulin resistance, thereby disproportionately increasing the CVD risk burden in these individuals [, ]. Collectively, our results provide a mechanistic framework linking vitamin D status to cardiovascular outcomes in asthma through these modifiable intermediate phenotypes.

Our study has several strengths. First, our findings are based on large-scale prospective data with long-term follow-up. This study aimed to investigate the effect of serum 25(OH)D levels on cardiovascular health in patients with asthma. To determine whether genetic variants in the VDR, modify the protective effect of serum 25(OH)D on CVD outcomes, we performed an interaction analysis. Additionally, we examined potential interactions with demographic characteristics, including sex, age, race and ethnicity, education level, smoking status, alcohol intake frequency, dietary habits, and season of blood collection. Finally, a series of stratification and sensitivity analyses were conducted to validate and strengthen the main findings.

The uniqueness and clinical significance of our study lie in the fact that, unlike previous research focusing on the association between 25(OH)D and the onset or control of asthma, this is the first investigation to examine the effects of both serum 25(OH)D levels and genetic variants in VDR on chronic CVD outcomes among asthma patients. Our findings underscore the cardiovascular benefits of maintaining 25(OH)D levels at or above 50 nmol/L in this population. Incorporating routine 25(OH)D monitoring into clinical guidelines may therefore improve asthma management strategies. This study provides clinical data to support effective interventions aimed at mitigating long-term adverse outcomes in asthma.

Our study has its limitations. First, its observational design limits causal inference. Second, serum 25(OH)D was measured by electrochemiluminescence immunoassay rather than the gold standard, and only a single baseline measurement was available, preventing assessment of longitudinal changes. Third, most participants were of European origin, limiting generalizability. Future studies in more diverse populations and with repeated measurements are needed to validate our findings and to further explore the role of 25(OH)D in different CVD subtypes and other comorbidities, as well as its potential as a biomarker in asthma management.

This large cohort of asthma patients demonstrated a significant L-shaped association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk, with a threshold around 50 nmol/L. This association was significantly mediated by BMI, systemic inflammation (CRP), and HbA1c. Furthermore, VDR polymorphisms ( BsmI , TaqI , and ApaI ) modified this association only under severe vitamin D deficiency. These findings highlight the potential importance of maintaining adequate 25(OH)D as a modifiable factor for CVD prevention in asthma and support consideration of 25(OH)D monitoring in long-term management strategies.

title: Could we diagnose childhood asthma by LIBS technique?
abstract: Asthma affects children related to trace elements. Our aim was to investigate the levels of trace elements using laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS). The study included 120 children aged 4-12 years from both sexes. They were divided into three groups: Group 1 of 40 children was diagnosed as cases of controlled asthma. Group 2 consisted of 40 children diagnosed as cases of uncontrolled asthma. Group 3 consisted of 40 children as normal control. Asthmatic children were classified according to GINA 2015. They were analyzed for serum levels of total IgE, eosinophil count, and trace metals (Zn, Cu, Pb, Mg, and Fe) by using LIBS. There was significant decrease in serum levels of Zn, Mg and Fe in children with asthma than in normal children. There was a significant decrease in uncontrolled asthmatic children than in controlled asthmatic children. But the Cu and Pb concentration in children with asthma was significantly higher than that in normal children, and there was a significant increase in uncontrolled asthmatic children than in controlled asthmatic children. Furthermore, we examined the peak flow meter, eosinophil count, and total IgE and found that the peak flow metric study had shown a significant difference in controlled cases, total eosinophil count, and IgE; the difference was more significant in the uncontrolled group than in the controlled group, and the total levels were higher in the uncontrolled group. Asthma is a common pediatric disease that is related to deficiency of Fe, Zn, and Mg and occurs with increased Pb and Cu. LIBS is a safe and rapid technique that helps in detecting asthma.

The study included 120 children aged 4-12 years from both sexes. They were divided into three groups: Group 1 of 40 children was diagnosed as cases of controlled asthma. title: MUC1 attenuates neutrophilic airway inflammation in asthma by reducing NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis through the inhibition of the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Neutrophilic airway inflammation is a challenge in asthma management and is associated with poor patient prognosis. Mucin 1 (MUC1), which contains a cytoplasmic tail (MUC1-CT), has been found to mediate glucocorticoid sensitivity in asthma; however, its role in modulating neutrophilic airway inflammation in asthma remains unknown. METHODS: Human-induced sputum cells were collected from healthy participants (n = 12), patients with mild-to-moderate asthma (n = 34), and those with severe asthma (n = 18). In vitro human lung bronchial 1 epithelial cell line (BEAS-2B) was transfected with small interfering RNA against MUC1 (MUC1-siRNA) and then stimulated by lipopolysaccharide (LPS), where some cells were pretreated with a TLR4 inhibitor (TAK-242). In vivo mouse model of asthmatic neutrophil airway inflammation was induced by ovalbumin (OVA)/LPS. Some groups were intraperitoneally injected with MUC1-CT inhibitor (GO-203) and/or TAK-242 . RESULTS: The mRNA expression of MUC1 was downregulated in the induced sputum of patients with asthma and correlated with asthmatic neutrophilic airway inflammation. The mRNA expressions of TLR4, MyD88, nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3), caspase-1, interleukin (IL)-18, and IL-1β in induced sputum cells of patients with asthma were upregulated and related to the mRNA expression of MUC1. LPS activated the TLR4 pathway and NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis in BEAS-2B cells in vitro, which were significantly aggravated after MUC1-siRNA transfection. Furthermore, MUCl-CT interacted with TLR4, and the interaction between TLR4 and MyD88 was significantly increased after MUCl-siRNA transfection. Moreover, TAK-242 ameliorated TLR4/MyD88/nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathway activation, NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis, and neutrophilic inflammation exacerbated by MUC1 downregulation. GO-203 exacerbated TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway activation in vivo, and NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis reduced in a mouse model of asthmatic neutrophil airway inflammation induced by OVA/LPS; these pathological changes were partially alleviated after TAK-242 application. CONCLUSION: This study revealed that MUC1 downregulation plays an important role in asthmatic neutrophilic airway inflammation. MUC1-CT reduces NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis by inhibiting the activation of the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway, thereby attenuating neutrophil airway inflammation in patients with asthma.

sections.other:
Asthma is a heterogeneous chronic respiratory inflammatory disease characterized by reversible airflow limitation, mucus hypersecretion, and airway hyperresponsiveness. The incidence rate of asthma in different countries ranges from 1 to 18%. Asthma can be classified into different inflammatory endotypes based on the proportion of inflammatory cells in the induced sputum [, ]. Neutrophilic asthma accounts for approximately 20–30% of all adult asthma cases []. Moreover, patients with asthma having neutrophilic airway inflammation frequently present with more late-onset, severe, or steroid-resistant asthma and are difficult to treat [, ]. Thus, the possible mechanism and effective therapeutic targets for neutrophilic airway inflammation should be explored in patients with asthma.

Pyroptosis is a proinflammatory programmed cell death characterized by cell lysis and proinflammatory cytokine release []. Notably, nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome-mediated caspase-1 activation is the canonical pathway of pyroptosis [, ]. Increasing evidence has demonstrated the important role of NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis in asthmatic neutrophilic airway inflammation. Simpson et al. [] revealed significantly elevated gene expression of NLRP3, caspase-1, and interleukin (IL)-1β in induced sputum of patients with neutrophilic asthma. Richard Y Kim et al. [] proposed that neutrophilic airway inflammation, disease severity, and steroid resistance in asthma were correlated with NLRP3 and IL-1β expression. Furthermore, inhibition of NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis has been reported to ameliorate airway neutrophilic inflammation in a murine asthma model [, ].

Mucin 1 (MUC1), a transmembrane glycoprotein in the mucin family, primarily consists of two noncovalently bound subunits, i.e., an N-terminal extracellular subunit and a C‐terminal subunit containing a cytoplasmic tail (MUC1‐CT). Unlike most other membrane-bound mucins, MUC1 is not only expressed in various epithelial cells but also in immune cells, such as neutrophils and macrophages []. Moreover, MUC1-CT can be shed from the cell membrane, interact with cell membrane receptors, or undergo nuclear translocation to regulate cell signal transduction [, ]. In recent years, several studies have revealed that MUC1 has a potent anti-inflammatory function in the respiratory system [, ], and its role in asthma has also received some attention. Javier Milara et al. [] revealed downregulated MUC1 expression in bronchial epithelial cells and peripheral blood neutrophils of patients with severe asthma, which was inversely correlated with daily doses of inhaled corticosteroids. Based on the theory that correct MUC1-CT/GRα complex formation and nuclear translocation are important to enhance corticosteroid anti-inflammatory inducible genes, they proposed that MUC1 deficiency impairs corticosteroid insensitivity in patients with asthma []. Some studies have revealed that MUC1 can regulate some programmed cell death pathways, such as apoptosis [], necroptosis [, ], and ferroptosis []. However, the influence of MUC1 on NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis remains unknown.

Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), which is the earliest discovered pattern recognition receptor in the TLR family, plays an important role in immune system function and inflammatory diseases []. Studies have revealed that TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway suppression can attenuate pathological mechanisms of asthma [, ]. Previous studies have reported that TLR4 is the upstream signal of NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and TLR4 can interact with its downstream partner myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88) on the cell membrane and activate nuclear factor kappa-light-chain enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) to stimulate pyroptosis in various cell types [, , ]. Furthermore, studies have revealed that MUC1 is an upstream regulator of the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB signaling pathway [, ].

This study aimed to explore the influence of MUC1 on neutrophil airway inflammation in patients with asthma and verify the underlying mechanism associated with the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway and NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis.

sections.methods:
Adult patients with physician-diagnosed asthma were recruited if they met the following inclusion criteria: recurrent episodes of wheezing, dyspnea, cough, and sputum production; either methacholine PD20 of < 2.505 mg or bronchodilation FEV1 change of > 200 mL; and 12% successfully induced sputum. The exclusion criteria were as follows: smokers, including those who quit smoking for < 6 months; those with an acute exacerbation in the last 1 month; those with respiratory infection in the last 2 weeks; those comorbid with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bronchiectasis, or interstitial pneumonia; those who were pregnant or breastfeeding; and those recently diagnosed with lung cancer or other solid organ malignancy. Asthma severity was retrospectively assessed based on the treatment level required to control symptoms at least 2–3 months according to the Global Initiative for Asthma 2021 []. Severe asthma (SA) is asthma which requires optimized treatment with high-dose ICS/LABA to prevent it from becoming uncontrolled or which remains uncontrolled despite such treatment. Healthy controls (HC) had no history of smoking for the last 6 months; no family history of asthma; no history of chronic respiratory disease and respiratory infection in the last 2 weeks; and no severe systemic disease. The induced sputum cells and supernatant of the participants were stored at − 80 °C for subsequent experiments.

All participants provided informed consent. The Ethics Committee of Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology approved the study.

Human bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2B, ATCC; Manassas, VA, USA) were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (Gibco, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco, USA) in a 5% CO 2 atmosphere at 37 °C. Cells were stimulated with 5 µg/mL of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Cat #: L2880, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) and 100 nM of TAK-242 (Cat #: HY-11,109, MedChemExpress, NJ, USA), and TAK-242 was preadded to the medium 2 h before LPS.

Cells were inoculated in 96-well plates at a density of 5 × 10 3 cells/well, and the culture supernatants were collected after drug treatment according to experimental requirements. Then, the LDH Cytotoxicity Assay Kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) was used to quantify LDH release in the cell culture supernatant following the manufacturer’s instructions. Absorbance at 490 nm was measured using a microplate reader.

The transfection reagent lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) was used to transfect BEAS-2B cells with human MUC1-siRNAs or NC-siRNA (Guangzhou, China) for 24 h. The MUC1-siRNA sequence was 5′-GTTCAGTGCCCAGCTCTAC-3′.

Female C57BL/6J mice (6–8 weeks old) were obtained from Gempharmatech (Jiangsu, China). All animals were maintained in a specific pathogen-free facility with free access to standard fodder and water and kept in a controlled environment (22 °C ± 2 °C, 55% ± 5% humidity) under a 12-h light/dark cycle. The animal protocols were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee at the Tongji Hospital (Certificate number: TJH-202,209,007, Approval date: September 2022 to November 2022).

Mice were divided into four groups (n = 6/group): control, OVA/LPS, OVA/LPS + GO-203, and OVA/LPS + GO-203 + TAK-242. Mice in the OVA/LPS, OVA/LPS + GO-203, and OVA/LPS + GO-203 + TAK-242 groups were sensitized by intraperitoneally injecting 100 µg of sensitized grade V OVA (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) and 1 mg of aluminum hydroxide (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) on days 0, 7, and 14. Subsequently, the sensitized animals were intranasally administered with 75 µg of OVA and 3.5 µg of LPS on days 21, 22, and 23. Mice in the control group were intraperitoneally injected and intranasally administered with an equal volume of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) on the corresponding days. Mice in the OVA/LPS + GO-203 and OVA/LPS + GO-203 + TAK-242 groups were intraperitoneally injected with the MUC1 inhibitor GO-203 (MedChemExpress, NJ, USA) (20 mg/kg) 2 h before each challenge. Mice in the OVA/LPS and OVA/LPS + GO-203 groups were intraperitoneally injected with PBS. Mice in the OVA/LPS + GO-203 + TAK-242 group were intraperitoneally injected with the TLR4 inhibitor TAK-242 (MedChemExpress, NJ, USA) (3 mg/kg) 2 h before the challenge. The mice in the other groups were intraperitoneally injected with the same volume and concentration of DMSO solvent. All mice were anesthetized, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) and lung tissue were collected for subsequent experiments on day 24.

The lung tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h. Then, the sections were embedded in paraffin, cut into 4-µm-thick sections, and subjected to H&E staining. The scoring criteria for peribronchial inflammation were as follows: 0, no inflammatory cells; 1, a small number of cells; 2, one layer of cells; 3, 2–4 layers of cells; and 4, > 4 layers of cells around the bronchi. The lung tissue sections were subjected to PAS staining to determine the abundance of PAS-positive cells in the airway and scored as follows: 0, the proportion of the positive cells of < 5%; 1, 5–25%; 2, 25–50%; 3, 50–75%; and 4, > 75%.

Trizol reagent (Takara Co., Dalian, China) was used to extract the total RNA from induced sputum cells, BEAS-2B cells, or lung tissues, and PrimeScript RT reagent Kit (Takara) was used for reverse transcription in the first-strand cDNA synthesis reaction. An SYBR Premix Ex Taq (Takara) was used for PCR reaction on Bio-Rad C1000 Thermal Cycler. The relative mRNA expression was analyzed using the 2 −ΔΔCt method, and the expression level was presented as fold change relative to the control. Primer sequences were synthesized by Sangon Biotech (Shanghai, China) (Table ).

Total protein was extracted from cultured cells and lung tissues using RIPA lysis buffer (Aspen Biological, Wuhan, China). The Nuclear and Cytoplasmic Protein Extraction Kit (Boster Biotech, Wuhan, China) was used to extract cytoplasmic and nuclear protein. BCA (Aspen) was used to measure protein concentration. The protein samples were separated via 12.5 SDS-PAGE (Yeasen Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) and then transferred onto polyvinylidene fluoride membranes (Roche, UK). Subsequently, the membranes were blocked with 5% nonfat dried milk in Tris-buffered saline with Tween 20 (TBST) for 90 min at 25 °C. Then, the membranes were incubated in the corresponding primary antibody overnight at 4 °C on a shaker. Subsequently, the membranes were washed using TBST and incubated with an appropriate HRP-labeled secondary antibody for 90 min at room temperature on a shaker. Thereafter, a ChemiDoc XRS gel imaging system (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) was used to assay the membranes that were washed again with TBST. Image J (NIH Image, Bethesda, MD) was used to quantitatively analyze the protein bands. GAPDH was included as a reference. Table shows the primary antibodies used for western blotting.

CO-IP proteins were extracted from cultured cells using NP40 lysis buffer (#B1027,Wuhan Promoter Biological CO., LTD). Equal amounts of protein aliquots of cell lysates were incubated overnight at 4 °C with immunoprecipitating antibody against MUC1-CT, MyD88, TLR4, or rabbit IgG (Abmart, B30011 ). Subsequently, protein A/G agarose beads (Abmart, Shanghai, China; A10001) were added and incubated together for 2 h. Then, the beads were washed with lysis buffer and eluted by boiling in loading buffer. Immunoprecipitated proteins were subjected to immunoblot analysis for the protein of interest. HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG heavy chain (Abclone, AS063) was used as the secondary antibody for CO-IP.

BEAS-2B cell climbing films and lung tissue paraffin sections were immunostained according to the instructions of the Universal IF Toolkit (Abkine, Wuhan, China). In brief, BEAS-2B cell climbing films were washed twice with PBS, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 30 min, and rinsed with PBS. Afterward, the cell slides were incubated with immunostaining permeabilization buffer at room temperature for 40 min. The paraffin section was dewaxed in xylene and ethanol with gradient concentration, and then the antigen was repaired with EDTA antigen retrieval solution at a pH of 8.0 in microwave oven and washed with PBS. Subsequently, the cell slides or lung tissue sections were incubated with goat serum blocking buffer for 40 min at room temperature and with corresponding primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. The next day, the cell slides or tissue sections were washed with antibody wash buffer and incubated with the corresponding fluorescent secondary antibody (Dylight 488 or A594, Goat Anti-Rabbit-IgG) for 1 h in dark. Then, they were re-stained with DAPI for 15 min and sealed with superKine™ snhanced antifade mounting medium. The slides or sections were visualized at ×400 under a microscope.

Data analysis was performed using the GraphPad Prism 9 software (GraphPad, San Diego, California). Normally distributed data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and student’s t-test or one-way analysis of variance was used to compare these data among the groups. Non-normally distributed data are presented as median (Q1, Q3); Kruskal–Wallis analysis was used to compare these data among the groups, and Spearman’s rank order correlation was used for correlation analysis. Two-sided p -values of < 0.05 were considered statistically significant and expressed as * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001; and **** p < 0.0001.
sections.results:
First, we collected induced sputum samples from 64 patients to detect whether MUC1 expression is altered in the airways of patients with asthma. Table summarizes the patient characteristics. No significant differences were found in age, sex, and body mass index among the healthy (n = 12), mild-to-moderate asthma (MMA) (n = 34), and SA (n = 18) groups. The forced vital capacity in the first second (FEV1) of the SA group was significantly lower than that of the MMA group. The predicted FEV 1 % of the SA group was significantly lower than that of the healthy and MMA groups. The forced vital capacity in the first second/forced vital capacity (FEV 1 /FVC) of the SA group was significantly lower than that of the healthy group. The proportion of neutrophils in the induced sputum of the MMA and SA groups was higher than that in the induced sputum of the healthy group, and the proportion of SA was significantly higher than that of MMA.

RT-qPCR was performed to detect MUC1 expression in induced sputum cells. The mRNA expression of MUC1 was notably downregulated in induced sputum cells of patients with SA compared with those of patients with HC and MMA (Fig. A). The mRNA expression of MUC1 in induced sputum cells was negatively correlated with FEV1 (% predicted) and FEV 1 /FVC for patients with asthma (n = 52) (Fig. B and C) and positively correlated with the proportion of neutrophils in induced sputum (Fig. D). These results indicated that the mRNA expression of MUC1 was downregulated in the induced sputum cells of patients with asthma and negatively correlated with NA severity.

RT-qPCR was performed to detect the mRNA expression of TLR4, MyD88 and NLRP3, caspase-1, and IL-1β in induced sputum cells. The mRNA expression of TLR4, MyD88, NLRP3, caspase-1, IL-18, and IL-1β in induced sputum cells was significantly increased compared with that in patients with HC and MMA (Fig. A-I). Moreover, the mRNA expression of MUC1 was positively correlated with the mRNA expression of TLR4, MyD88, NLRP3, caspase-1 IL-18, and IL-1β (Fig. G-L).

We stimulated BEAS-2B cells with LPS for 24 h in vitro to determine whether LPS affects the expression of MUC1 in BEAS-2B cells and found increased mRNA and protein expressions of MUC1 (Fig. A and B). Meanwhile, TLR4, MyD88 protein expression, and p65 phosphorylation level were upregulated in the LPS group compared with the control group (Fig. C). Furthermore, LPS increased the protein expression of NLRP3, caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1, GSDMD, GSDMD-N, IL-18, and IL-1β in cells (Fig. D) as well as increased the release of LDH (Fig. E), indicating that LPS induced pyroptosis in BEAS-2B cells. In addition, LPS increased the mRNA expression levels of the inflammatory factors IL-6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-1β, and TNF-α (Fig. F), triggering the inflammatory response of BEAS-2B cells.

To demonstrate the effect of MUC1 on the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway and pyroptosis, BEAS-2B cells were transfected with MUC1-siRNA for 24 h before LPS intervention. Compared with the control and NC-siRNA groups, the mRNA and protein expression levels of MUC1 in the MUC1-siRNA group were significantly decreased (Fig. A and B). Compared with the NC-siRNA + LPS group, the protein expression levels of TLR4, MyD88, and p-p65 in the MUC1-siRNA + LPS group increased, and the p65 protein level in the nucleus also increased (Fig. C and D). Moreover, immunofluorescence staining of the cell slides revealed that the relative fluorescence intensity of p-p65 in the MUC1-siRNA + LPS group was increased (Fig. E). For pyroptosis, we found that LPS-induced NLRP3, caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1, GSDMD, GSDMD-N, IL-18, and IL-1β protein expression levels were further increased after MUC1 knockdown (Fig. H), and the LDH level in the cell supernatant was also further increased (Fig. I). At the same time, the mRNA expression levels of the inflammatory factors IL-6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-1β, and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α in BEAS-2B cells further increased after MUC1 knockdown (Fig. J). These results revealed that MUC1 knockdown facilitates TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway activation, increases NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis, and aggravates inflammatory response, thereby indicating the protective role of MUC1 in asthma. Previous studies have revealed that MUC1 can competitively bind TLR5 and TLR3 with MyD88 through its cytoplasmic tail domain (MUC1-CT), thereby inhibiting NF-κB activation [, ]. Here, we used the CO-IP method to detect a protein interaction between MUC1-CT and TLR4 in BEAS-2B cells, and LPS enhanced their binding (Fig. F). Moreover, the binding of TLR4 and MyD88 significantly increased after MUC1-siRNA transfection, indicating that MUC1-CT can hinder the TLR4 and MyD88 binding (Fig. G).

Finally, we aimed to confirm the association between the inhibitory effect of MUC1 on pyroptosis and TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway activation downregulation in vitro. We pretreated the cells with TAK-242, a specific TLR4 inhibitor, for 2 h before LPS stimulation. We found that TAK-242 pretreatment did not affect the expression level of MUCl (Fig. A and B). The expression of TLR4, MyD88, and p-p65 in the MUC1-siRNA + LPS + TAK-242 group was significantly reduced (Fig. C); moreover, nuclear p65 level (Fig. D) and the intensity of immunofluorescence for p-p65 (Fig. E) were reduced compared with the those in MUC1-siRNA + LPS group. Concurrently, the protein expression levels of NLRP3, caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1, GSDMD, GSDMD-N, IL-18, IL-1β, and LDH in the culture medium of the MUC1-siRNA + LPS + TAK-242 group were significantly lower than those of the MUC1-siRNA + LPS group (Fig. Fand G). The increased mRNA expression levels of the inflammatory factors IL-6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-1β, and TNF-α caused by MUC1 knockdown were partially reversed (Fig. H) after TAK-242 pretreatment. These results suggest that the protective effect of MUC1 against NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis and inflammation is related to its ability to block TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway activation.

Previous studies have revealed that the anti-inflammatory activity of MUC1 in TLR pathway activation mainly depends on its intracellular cytoplasmic tail (MUC1-CT) inhibition [, ]. GO-203, an analog of MUC1-CT, can penetrate the cell membrane and bind to the CQC motif of MUC-CT, thereby blocking its intracellular signal transduction function [] and the TLR pathway regulation function [, ]. We induced C57BL/6J mice with OVA/LPS to establish a sthmatic models and used GO-203 and TAK-242 to block the MUC1 and TLR4 functions, respectively, to verify the results obtained in cell experiments in vivo. The results were consistent with what we expected. The inflammation around the airway, goblet cell hyperplasia, inflammation score, and PAS score in the OVA/LPS + GO-203 group (Fig. A and B) were significantly increased compared with the OVA/LPS group (Fig. C and D). The total number and differential counts of inflammatory cells in the BALF significantly increased, with the most significant increase observed in neutrophils, in the BALF of mice in the OVA/LPS + GO-203 group (Fig. E). Concurrently, the mRNA expressions of the inflammatory factors IL-6, IL-8, IL-18, IL-1β, and TNF-α in the lung tissue of mice in the OVA/LPS + GO-203 group were significantly increased (Fig. F). These results indicated that GO-203 blocked the function of MUC1-CT to aggravate neutrophil inflammation in the airways of OVA/LPS-induced asthmatic mouse, suggesting the protective effect of MUC1 on neutrophilic airway inflammation in patients with asthma. Comparison of the OVA/LPS + GO-203 and OVA/LPS + GO-203 + TAK-242 groups revealed that the abovementioned airway inflammation indicators were significantly suppressed in the OVA/LPS + GO-203 + TAK-242 group. Furthermore, we observed that TAK-242 partially reversed the increased neutrophilic airway inflammation caused by MUC1 function inhibition in OVA/LPS-induced asthmatic mouse.

We found that the expression level of MUC1 was decreased in the OVA/LPS group compared with the control group (Fig. A and B), whereas the expression levels of TLR4, MyD88, p-p65, and nuclear p65 (Fig. A-C) were significantly increased, as detected via western blotting and immunofluorescence staining. In addition, the protein expression levels of NLRP3, caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1, GSDMD, GSDMD-N, IL-18, and IL-1β (Fig. D and E) were increased, indicating that MUC1, TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway, and NLRP3-induced pyroptosis are involved in the pathogenesis of asthma. The protein expression levels of TLR4, MyD88, and p-p65 in the lung tissue as well as nuclear p65 level of mice in the OVA/LPS + GO-203 group were significantly increased compared with the OVA/LPS group (Fig. C). Moreover, the LDH level in the OVA/LPS + GO-203 group was significantly higher than that in the OVA/LPS group (Fig. E), and the protein expression levels of NLRP3, caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1, GSDMD, GSDMD-N, IL-18, and IL-1β were significantly increased (Fig. D and E). These results indicated that significant inhibition of the signal transduction function of MUC1 facilitates TLR4/MyD88/p-p65 pathway activation and NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis. Furthermore, TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway activation and NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis were simultaneously inhibited in the OVA/LPS + GO-203 group compared with the OVA/LPS + GO-203 group. Overall, TAK-242 downregulates GO-203-caused TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway activation and NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis in OVA/LPS-induced asthmatic mouse.
sections.discussion:
Neutrophilic airway inflammation is considered an important issue in asthma management and is often accompanied by corticosteroid resistance, progressive lung function decline, and frequent asthma exacerbations []. At present, treatment methods for asthma mainly target eosinophilic inflammation, and the symptom control of patients with asthma having neutrophilic airway inflammation is often not satisfactory. Therefore, the underlying mechanism and alternative therapeutic targets for neutrophilic airway inflammation in asthma should be explored.

MUC1 has been considered to have a potential value in the treatment of SA because of its role in regulating the sensitivity of glucocorticoids []. However, neutrophilic airway inflammation regulation by MUC1 is unclear in asthma. The present study revealed that MUC1 expression in induced sputum of patients with asthma was downregulated and was related to asthma severity. This is consistent with the results of a previous study on human bronchial epithelial cells and blood neutrophils []. Moreover, we discovered that MUC1 expression was significantly negatively correlated with the proportion of neutrophils in induced sputum of patients with asthma, indicating that MUC1 may have an inhibitory effect on neutrophil airway inflammation in asthma. We did not perform bronchial biopsy and collect airway epithelial cells from the participants, which may represent a limitation of this study, considering ethics and patient acceptance. However, a previous study [] reported changes in the expression levels of MUC1 in bronchial epithelial cells and blood neutrophils of patients with asthma, and our study supplemented the changes in induced sputum cells. Interestingly, Anil KM et al. [] found that MUC1 expression was upregulated in most patients with asthma who were sensitive and exposed to a pigeon allergen. Their results are inconsistent with our results, possibly due to the following reasons: First, the samples they collected and the MUC1 structural fragments they detected were different from those in our study. They detected the protein expression of the circulating form of MUC1, a sialylated sugar chain of the MUC1 ectodomain, in the serum, whereas we detected MUC1 gene expression in induced sputum cells. Second, their study did not include a healthy control group for comparison with patients with asthma. Moreover, they did they group and compare patients according to the severity of asthma, as performed in our study. In addition, they compared patients with asthma with positive and negative pigeon allergens and found that MUC1 expression in the serum of patients with positive pigeon allergens was higher than that in the serum of patients with negative pigeon allergens, suggesting that the circulating form of MUC1 is a biomarker in pigeon-sensitive asthma patients []. However, the mechanism by which the circulating form of MUC1 is upregulated in patients with positive pigeon allergens remains unknown and is worth exploring in the future.

NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis has been thought to be an important trigger of neutrophil airway inflammation in asthma [–]. Previous studies have reported that TLR4 can promote NF-κB activation by interacting with the adapter molecule MyD88, induce NLRP3 inflammasome and caspase-1 activation, and trigger pyroptosis [–]. Concurrently, the negative regulatory effect of MUC1 on the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway has been described in other diseases, such as acute lung injury and acute kidney injury [, ]. However, whether MUC1 regulates NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis through the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway in asthma remains unknown. We examined the expression levels of TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway- and NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis-related molecules in induced sputum cells. The results revealed that the expression of these molecules in induced sputum cells of patients with asthma was significantly increased compared with that in healthy subjects. Furthermore, consistent with our hypothesis, the expression of these molecules was significantly negatively correlated with the expression of MUC1.

We discovered that NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis was significantly increased after the reduction of MUC1 expression in in vitro experiments through stimulation of BEAS-2B with LPS and successive transfecton with MUC1-siRNA; this revealed the potential of MUC1 in reducing neutrophilic inflammation in asthma that was closely related to NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated-pyroptosis. Previous studies have revealed that MUC1 can inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation in Helicobacter pylori gastritis and bacterial infection, but they mainly studied NLRP3 inflammasome as an inflammatory mediator [, ]. In contrast, this study regarded NLRP3 inflammasome activation as an initiation of pyroptosis and revealed the downregulation effect of MUC1 on pyroptosis in asthma. We further revealed that TLR4 inhibition attenuated the upregulation of pyroptosis induced by MUC1 knockdown using TAK-242. These results demonstrated that the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway was a bridge between MUC1 and NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis. Furthermore, this study adds to the evidence that MUC1 regulates the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway and NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis in patients with asthma.

However, the exact mechanism of how MUC1 regulates the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway is unclear. Protein interactions were reported between MUC1 and some TLRs, including TLR5, TLR3, and TLR9 [, , ]. Gibier, Jean-Baptiste et al. [] demonstrated the interaction between MUC1 and TLR4 in HEK-293 cells using proximity ligation assay and revealed that MUC1 can interact with TLR4 through its intracellular CT domain, act as a competitive inhibitor of MyD88, and reduce NF-κB activation. Therefore, we also detected the interaction between MUC1-CT and TLR4 using CO-IP in BEAS-2B cells and found that MyD88 recruited by TLR4 was significantly increased in BEAS-2B cells stimulated with LPS after MUC1 knockdown. These results indicate that the interaction between MUC1-CT and TLR4 is one of the mechanisms for MUC1 to regulate the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway. Moreover, the expression of TLR4 was significantly upregulated after transfection with MUC1-siRNA, consistent with other studies [, ]. Yu-Ming Wang recently reported that MUC1 inhibited the expression of TLR4 by stabilizing the transcription factor HIF-α []. We did not verify this nor did we deeply explore other possible mechanisms by which MUC1 affects the expression level of TLR4; this can be a topic for future research.

GO-203, an analog of MUC1-CT, can bind to the CQC motif of MUC-CT, thereby blocking its intracellular signal transduction function [] and the regulation function of the TLR pathway [, ]. Finally, intraperitoneal injection with GO-203 in OVA/LPS-induced asthmatic mice aggravated neutrophil inflammation in their airways and increased TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway activation and NLPP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis. Moreover, TAK-242, a specific TLR4 inhibitor, partially reversed this change. Consistent with the in vitro results, these in vivo results more intuitively clarified the role of MUC1 in reducing neutrophilic airway inflammation in asthma. However, economic conditions to construct a MUC1 knockout mouse model were insufficient, being a limitation of this study. Fortunately, many studies have recognized the inhibitory effect of GO-203 on MUC1-CT in the lung [, ].

This study explored the inhibitory effect of MUC1 on NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis in patients with asthma and revealed that one of the underlying mechanisms is the downregulation of TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway activation. Several previous studies have suggested that neutrophilic airway inflammation in asthma may be effectively reduced by blocking NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis [, , ]; however, the results of clinical trials have been disappointing. For example, clinical trials of the NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 were halted due to its toxicity []. Canakinumab, an IL-1β monoclonal antibody, is no longer being studied as a therapeutic drug for asthma because of its complicated mechanism and unsatisfactory effect []. The role of some other pyroptosis inhibitors in asthma remains unclear. Therefore, the results of this study are clinically significant. We explored a long signaling pathway involved in neutrophil airway inflammation in asthma, which offers many alternative therapeutic targets for neutrophilic asthma. Targeting the upstream of NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis and simultaneously inhibiting multiple targets may have a better therapeutic effect on neutrophil airway inflammation in asthma.

The greatest significance of this study is to reveal the potential protective role of MUC1 in neutrophil airway inflammation in patients with asthma. In general, neutrophilic airway inflammation and glucocorticoid resistance are important factors for poor asthma control, and an inherent correlation exists between the two []. Previous studies have demonstrated that MUC1 deficiency mediates corticosteroid insensitivity in patients with asthma [, ]. This study shows the role of MUC1 in attenuating neutrophil-induced airway inflammation, further emphasizing the importance of MUC1 in the pathogenesis of asthma, which may have a potential value for developing new treatment strategies for refractory asthma. However, the reason for MUC1 expression downregulation in the course of asthma remains unknown, and more research may be needed in the future to prevent MUC1 deficiency or increase MUC1 expression in asthma.

In summary, this study revealed that MUC1 was downregulated in induced sputum of patients with asthma and played an important role in neutrophilic airway inflammation. Mechanistic studies revealed that MUC1 reduced NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis by inhibiting TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway activation, thereby suppressing neutrophilic airway inflammation in patients with asthma. This study suggested a possible mechanism of neutrophilic airway inflammation in patients with asthma and emphasized the anti-inflammatory function of MUC1 in neutrophilic asthma, thereby indicating that MUC1 is of a potential value to develop new asthma treatment strategies.

title: Asthma and Fixed Airways Obstruction: Real Life Aspects.
abstract: We aimed to evaluate asthmatic patients with fixed airways obstruction (FAO) and to verify the impact of follow-up in an asthma-dedicated outpatient clinic on symptoms control and spirometry compared to asthmatics without FAO. We enrolled 20 asthmatic FAO+ patients and 20 FAO- asthmatics at baseline (T0) and at a one-year follow-up visit (T1). FAO+ and FAO- groups were compared for anamnesis, FEV1, asthma control test (ACT) and their ΔT0-T1. FAO+ and FAO- groups did not differ for age, BMI, pack-years, allergy, T0 blood eosinophils, comorbidities or GINA therapy step at T0 and T1, whereas, in the FAO+ group, we found more patients with a delay >5 years between symptoms onset and correct asthma diagnosis (p < 0.05). ACT at T0 and ΔT0-T1, FEV1 at ΔT0-T1 and number of exacerbations at T0 and ΔT0-T1 did not differ between groups. Despite a widespread perception of FAO, per se, as a severity factor for asthma, we found similar severity profiles and amelioration after one year of treatment in the FAO+ and FAO- groups. The only factor linked to FAO development in our population was a delay in asthma diagnosis from respiratory symptoms onset, which may have led to airway remodeling. Physicians should characterize patients with FAO for avoiding misdiagnosis between asthma and other respiratory diseases and for establishing the appropriate therapy.

sections.abstract:
What are the main findings?

We found new aspects of fixed airways obstruction in severe asthma probably linked to late asthma diagnosis.

Asthma with and without fixed airways obstruction had similar outcomes.

What is the implication of the main finding?

A prompt differential diagnosis between severe asthma and COPD is essential.

The above is important to avoid further airway remodeling.
