sections.results:
Oral health is a fundamental determinant of overall health and an important contributor to quality of life, as it influences essential daily functions such as speaking, eating, smiling and contributes significantly to children’s social and emotional development []. Traditional clinical indicators of oral disease, or “normative” assessments, provide limited insight into the broader consequences of oral conditions on children’s lives [,]. To address this limitation, oral health-related quality of life (OHRQoL) has been extensively used as a multidimensional measure of the impact of oral diseases and disorders on individuals and communities []. Unlike normative assessments, OHRQoL instruments capture subjective experiences and the psychosocial consequences of oral conditions, reflecting patients’ perspectives and their families []. Such measures are also useful as outcomes in evaluating dental interventions and for identifying patient-centered needs [].

Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) indices have been increasingly integrated into disease surveillance systems [], enabling morbidity comparisons and guiding health policy priorities. Dental caries, despite significant advances in prevention and treatment, remains one of the most prevalent chronic diseases of childhood. Globally, an estimated 532 million children have untreated caries in primary teeth []. Gingivitis is also highly prevalent, with severity and extent increasing with age, peaking during puberty before a modest decline in adolescence [,]. Malocclusion is another frequent condition, with several epidemiological studies reporting high prevalence and growing demand for orthodontic care among children [,]. In addition to behavioral and individual factors, social determinants play a key role in shaping the prevalence and severity of oral diseases. Caries represents not only a health condition but also a social problem, disproportionately affecting socioeconomically disadvantaged populations []. Children from families with lower socioeconomic status tend to have poorer OHRQoL, ref. [], reflecting both reduced capacity to access and respond to oral health problems and differences in perception of their health needs.

Asthma is a common chronic respiratory disease, with a prevalence ranging between 1% and 29% worldwide []. In Portugal, data from the INAsma survey report an estimated prevalence of 8.4% among children []. Beyond respiratory symptoms, asthma impacts daily functioning, psychological well-being, and overall quality of life for children and their families [].

Several studies have examined the potential impact of asthma and its pharmacological management on the oral health of children and adolescents []. Asthmatic individuals frequently present with oral mucosal dehydration, reduced salivary flow, and lower oral pH, often associated with habitual mouth breathing, a common characteristic of this condition, as well as with the side effects of medications that diminish salivary secretion and alter salivary composition [,]. Moreover, some asthma medications, contain sugar further increasing susceptibility to oral health problems. The reported oral findings include increased incidence of dental caries, tooth wear, gingivitis, and an altered salivary composition and flow rate [,].

Asthma and its treatment may influence oral health through multiple pathways, including reduced salivary flow, altered oral pH, and mouth breathing. These changes may increase susceptibility to dental caries and oral discomfort, which in turn may affect daily functions such as eating and speaking, ultimately impacting OHRQoL. Nevertheless, the available evidence remains inconsistent and potentially confounded by factors such as socioeconomic status, dietary patterns, and methodological heterogeneity across studies [,]. While several investigations have focused on the clinical oral health of children with asthma, relatively few have examined its association with oral health–related quality of life (OHRQoL). Evidence addressing this relationship in Portuguese pediatric populations is scarce. Therefore, the present study was designed to address this gap by investigating OHRQoL and clinical oral health indicators in Portuguese children aged 6 to 8 years with and without asthma, using the validated Portuguese version of the SOHO-5. To our knowledge, this is the first study to specifically examine the association between asthma and OHRQoL in this age group using a child self-report instrument in a Portuguese population.

The primary aim of this study was to evaluate oral health-related quality of life (OHRQoL) in Portuguese children with asthma compared with non-asthmatic peers, using the SOHO-5 instrument. Secondary aims included comparing caries experience, salivary parameters, gingival health, and other clinical oral health indicators between the two groups.

This cross-sectional study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Dental Medicine, University of Lisbon (reference: 202326) and Ethics Committee of São José Local Health Unit (1512/2024). The study population consisted of children aged 6 to 8 years and their parents, recruited from the Lisbon metropolitan area. Both children with asthma and healthy controls were included.

An a priori sample size calculation was performed using G*Power software v.3.1 (Heinrich-Heine-Universität Düsseldorf, Düsseldorf, Germany). Parameters included a significance level (α) of 0.05, statistical power (1 − β) of 0.80, and a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.8), assumed in the absence of specific prior data on OHRQoL differences between asthmatic and non-asthmatic children in this age group and context. The analysis indicated that a minimum of 26 children per group would be required for the primary group comparison. It should be noted that this calculation was not designed to support subgroup or stratified analyses.

A non-probabilistic convenience sampling strategy was employed. Children clinically diagnosed with asthma and undergoing maintenance therapy with inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), with or without additional controller medications, were recruited from the Immunoallergology Service of D. Estefânia Children’s Hospital. Healthy controls were recruited from a primary school in Lisbon. Eligibility criteria for both groups were:

Age 6 to 8 years; Absence of other chronic illnesses; Not wearing orthodontic appliances; No systemic antibiotic use in the preceding two weeks.

Written informed consent was obtained from all parents, and verbal assent was obtained from the children.

For each child in the asthma group, the total daily dose of inhaled corticosteroids was recorded and classified as low, medium, or high according to the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) guidelines []. This categorization enabled a standardized evaluation of treatment intensity and allowed for the investigation of potential dose–response relationships with oral health–related outcomes.

Data were collected between June 2024 and July 2025. All clinical examinations were conducted by a single trained examiner, assisted by a recorder, ensuring consistency across assessments. Intraexaminer reliability was assessed in a subsample of 17 children. Cohen’s kappa coefficient for caries in primary teeth was 0.850, indicating very good agreement.

Child assessment: Children completed the Portuguese child self-report version of the SOHO-5 questionnaire [] and underwent intraoral examination.

Intraoral examination: Before clinical assessment, tooth surfaces were cleaned with gauze to facilitate visualization. Clinical assessments recorded the presence of dental caries (WHO criteria), incisor-molar hypomineralisation, dental erosion, oral mucosal lesions, malocclusion, spontaneous gingival bleeding, and visible bacterial plaque (Oral Hygiene Index-Simplified). Gingival bleeding was assessed at six sites per tooth (mesiobuccal, buccal, distobuccal, mesiolingual, lingual, and distolingual) using a periodontal probe with a ball-shaped tip, following the Bleeding on Probing (BOP) method as recommended by the World Health Organization []. In addition, stimulated saliva was collected over five minutes by having the child chew on a piece of sterile paraffin wax, and the volume was measured to assess salivary flow rate. A stimulated salivary flow rate below 1.0 mL/min was classified as low, based on established reference values for this age group [].

Parent questionnaire: A self-administered questionnaire collected sociodemographic information (age, sex, nationality, siblings, parental education), oral health behaviors (brushing frequency, fluoride toothpaste use, supervision, cariogenic food intake, previous dental visits), early-life health information, and the Portuguese parent version of the SOHO-5 [].

The clinical examination was conducted by a trained examiner, assisted by a recorder. Instruments included a mouth mirror (ASA reference 2200E-5, 24 mm diameter) and a periodontal probe with a ball-shaped tip (ASA reference 0702L-12S), following World Health Organization recommendations []. Illumination was provided by a white LED headlight. All procedures adhered to standard infection control protocols, including sterilization of instruments and the use of gloves and masks.

The SOHO-5 comprises two versions: a child self-report and a parent proxy-report, each containing 7 items. The child version covers difficulties in eating, drinking, speaking, playing, sleeping, and avoiding smiling due to pain or appearance concerns. Items are rated on a 3-point scale (0 = no; 1 = a little; 2 = a lot). The parent version assesses similar domains, with the addition of self-confidence, rated on a 5-point scale (0 = not at all to 4 = a great deal, plus “don’t know”). Questionnaires with more than two “don’t know” responses were excluded.

Scores range from 0 to 14 for the child version and 0 to 28 for the parent version, with higher scores indicating poorer OHRQoL []. The validated and culturally adapted Portuguese version of the SOHO-5 used in this study was adapted from the Brazilian Portuguese version [], with minor linguistic modifications to ensure cultural appropriateness []. Content validity was confirmed by an expert panel of three dentists (two Portuguese, one Brazilian) with relevant research experience. Psychometric analysis demonstrated good internal consistency, with Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.86 (child version), 0.83 (caregiver version), and 0.84 (total score), indicating high reliability []. Item-total correlations were moderate, with no items requiring exclusion. Test–retest reliability was assessed using the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC), yielding values of 0.82 for the child version and 0.95 for the total score, indicating good to excellent temporal reliability [].

Data were analyzed using SPSS, version 29 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Descriptive statistics were calculated for all variables. Continuous variables were described using mean and standard deviation (SD), median and interquartile range (Q1–Q3) when data were not normally distributed. Categorical variables were expressed as absolute frequencies and percentages.

Normality of distribution was assessed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. For group comparisons, the Chi-square test and Fisher’s Exact test were used for categorical variables, and the Mann–Whitney-U test was used for continuous non-normally distributed variables. Subgroup analyses were conducted within the asthma group to explore associations between clinical variables and OHRQoL scores.

To further examine the independent association between asthma and oral health outcomes, multivariable regression analyses were performed. Binary logistic regression was used for dichotomous outcomes (caries in primary teeth and low stimulated salivary flow), and linear regression for continuous outcomes (SOHO-5 child and total scores). To select covariates for inclusion in the final models, preliminary separate regression analyses were conducted examining sociodemographic, behavioral, and asthma-related variables as potential predictors of each outcome. Given the limited sample size and the need to maintain adequate event-per-variable ratios, the number of covariates in each final model was restricted to a maximum of two, in addition to the main exposure variable (presence of asthma). Based on this approach, pain experience in the past year and frequency of sugary drinks consumption were selected as covariates across all final models. Model fit for logistic regression models was assessed using the Hosmer–Lemeshow test and Nagelkerke R 2 , and for linear regression models using the F-test and R 2 .

A significance level of p < 0.05 was applied to all analyses.

The final sample comprised 89 child–parent pairs. Children had a mean age of 7.3 years (SD = 0.8); 57.7% were male, and 88.8% lived with both parents. University-level education was reported by 56% of mothers and 54% of fathers. Among the 38 children with asthma, 7.9% ( n = 3) were treated with low doses of ICS, 52.6% ( n = 20) medium doses of ICS, and 39.5% ( n = 15) with high doses of ICS. Regarding oral health behaviors, 75.3% of children attended regular dental check-ups, and 70.8% had visited a dentist within the previous six months. Dental pain in the past year was reported by 18%. Brushing twice daily was reported by 84.3%, use of fluoridated toothpaste by 83.1%, and daily flossing by 14.6%. Supervised brushing was reported by 61.8% of participants. Weekly consumption of sugary drinks and cariogenic foods was reported by 65.2% and 73%, respectively.

The prevalence of caries in deciduous dentition was 38.2% ( n = 34), with a mean dmft score of 1.8 (SD = 2.75). In permanent teeth, caries prevalence was 14% ( n = 12), with a mean DMFT of 0.35 (SD = 0.90). Other clinical findings included gingival bleeding (9%), molar–incisor hypomineralization (28.1%), and mild dental erosion (3.4%). Aphthous ulcers (4.5%) were the most common mucosal lesion. Malocclusion was also frequent: 48.7% presented a Class II molar relationship, 5.3% Class III, 14.6% crossbite, 16.9% open bite, and 15.7% deep bite. Stimulated salivary flow was <1.0 mL/min in 57.3% of children ().

Caries experience in the primary dentition was significantly higher among asthmatic children (52.6%) compared with non-asthmatic children (27.5%) ( p = 0.027). Notably, caries in permanent dentition occurred exclusively in the asthma group (32.4%), with no cases among non-asthmatic children ( p < 0.001) (). Although the absence of caries in permanent teeth among controls may partly reflect the young age of the sample—in which permanent dentition is not yet fully erupted—the difference between groups remained statistically significant and warrants attention.

The mean dmft was significantly higher in asthmatic children (2.68 ± 3.27) compared with controls (1.14 ± 2.08; p = 0.026). Asthmatic children also showed higher numbers of decayed primary teeth (2.05 ± 2.71 vs. 0.67 ± 1.63; p = 0.003) and missing primary teeth (0.37 ± 0.88 vs. 0.02 ± 0.14; p = 0.007). In the permanent dentition, asthmatic children had a significantly higher number of decayed teeth (0.57 ± 1.07; p < 0.001) and greater mean DMFT scores (0.73 ± 1.24; p < 0.001). No significant differences were observed between groups for gingival bleeding, molar–incisor hypomineralization, dental erosion, or oral mucosal alterations ( p > 0.05). Similarly, no differences were found in sagittal, transversal, or vertical malocclusion patterns ( p > 0.05).

Stimulated salivary flow < 1.0 mL/min was significantly more prevalent among asthmatic children (78.9%) compared with controls (41.2%; p < 0.001) ().

In the study sample ( n = 89), the child-reported score ranged from 0 to 9 (median 1.00 [Q1 = 0.00; Q3 = 3.00]; mean 1.75, SD = 1.98), the parent-reported score ranged from 0 to 14 (median 0.00 [Q1 = 0.00; Q3 = 1.00]; mean 1.20, SD = 2.58), and the total score ranged from 0 to 14 (median 2.00 [Q1 = 0.00; Q3 = 4.00]; mean 2.94, SD = 3.48). Asthmatic children consistently reported poorer OHRQoL compared with non-asthmatic peers across all three scores, reaching statistical significance for child-reported ( p = 0.004) and total scores ( p = 0.001), but not for parent-reported scores ( p = 0.059) ().

Although the absolute SOHO-5 scores were generally low in both groups—suggesting an overall favorable oral health-related quality of life—the statistically significant differences between groups indicate that asthmatic children experience a meaningfully greater burden in their daily oral health experiences, particularly in functional domains such as eating and speaking. Functional domains were most affected: “difficulty eating” and “difficulty speaking” in the child version, and “difficulty eating” and “difficulty sleeping” in the parent version. In the child-reported SOHO-5, the response ‘No’ was the most frequently endorsed across all items.

Significant differences were observed, particularly among 8-year-olds, where parent-reported and total scores were higher in the asthma group. Higher SOHO-5 scores were also associated with parental higher education and with the presence of caries. Dental pain was strongly associated with worse OHRQoL in both groups. Subgroup analysis revealed that asthmatic children with low salivary flow reported significantly poorer OHRQoL on both child-reported ( p = 0.009) and total scores ( p = 0.005), although parent-reported differences were not significant ( p = 0.104). ( and ) These subgroup analyses were not pre-specified in the original study design and should therefore be interpreted as exploratory. Given the small cell sizes and the increased risk of type II error, no definitive conclusions can be drawn from these findings.

Two binary logistic regression models were fitted for caries in primary teeth (EPV = 11.3) and low stimulated salivary flow (EPV = 12.7), and two linear regression models for SOHO-5 child and total scores. All models showed adequate fit. For caries in primary teeth, the logistic model explained approximately 38% of the variance (Nagelkerke R 2 = 0.380; Hosmer–Lemeshow: χ 2 = 4.321, p = 0.504). After adjustment, asthma was not a significant independent predictor (OR = 1.345, 95% CI: 0.457–3.958, p = 0.590), suggesting that the bivariate association may be partially confounded by dietary habits. Frequency of sugary drinks consumption was a significant predictor of higher caries odds (OR = 3.994, 95% CI: 1.357–11.753, p = 0.012). Pain experience in the past year was also a significant predictor of higher caries odds (OR = 14.250, 95% CI: 2.543–79.849, p = 0.003), likely reflecting greater dental disease burden in symptomatic children. For low salivary flow, the model explained approximately 28% of the variance (Nagelkerke R 2 = 0.277; Hosmer–Lemeshow: χ 2 = 5.088, p = 0.278). In contrast to caries, asthma remained a significant independent predictor of low salivary flow after adjustment (OR = 4.017, 95% CI: 1.443–11.178, p = 0.008), confirming that this association is not explained by behavioral confounders. Pain experience was also significant (OR = 10.907, 95% CI: 1.230–96.746, p = 0.032).

For OHRQoL outcomes, both linear models were statistically significant (SOHO-5 child: F(3,85) = 5.633, p = 0.001, R 2 = 0.166; SOHO-5 total: F(3,85) = 15.888, p < 0.001, R 2 = 0.359). Pain experience in the past year was the strongest predictor across both models (SOHO-5 child: B = 1.583, 95% CI: 0.473–2.693, p = 0.006; SOHO-5 total: B = 4.970, 95% CI: 3.266–6.673, p < 0.001), indicating that children with pain history reported substantially worse OHRQoL. Frequency of sugary drinks was not significant in either model ( p = 0.845; p = 0.882). After adjustment, asthma showed a borderline non-significant trend towards poorer child-reported OHRQoL (B = 0.732, 95% CI: −0.116 to 1.581, p = 0.090) and was not a significant predictor of total OHRQoL (B = 0.693, 95% CI: −0.609 to 1.996, p = 0.293). Detailed results are presented in .

This study examined the association between childhood asthma and oral health outcomes, including caries experience, salivary flow, and oral health-related quality of life (OHRQoL). The findings suggest that children with asthma may be at higher risk of certain oral health problems, including higher caries prevalence, higher dmft/DMFT indices, and reduced stimulated salivary flow. These clinical differences were associated with poorer OHRQoL, particularly from the child’s perspective. However, these associations should be interpreted with caution given the cross-sectional design, the convenience sampling strategy, and the differences in socioeconomic profile between groups observed in this study.

The higher caries prevalence observed among asthmatic children in the bivariate analysis is consistent with previous reports. Meta-analyses by Alavaikko et al. and Agostini et al. have reported an approximately 1.5-fold increased risk of caries in children with asthma [,]. However, the multivariable analysis conducted in the present study suggests that this association may be partially confounded by dietary habits—specifically, frequency of sugary drinks consumption—rather than reflecting a direct effect of asthma per se (OR = 1.345, p = 0.590 after adjustment). This finding is consistent with evidence highlighting the role of behavioral and socioeconomic confounders in the relationship between asthma and caries [] and underscores the need for caution when interpreting bivariate associations in this context.

The markedly higher prevalence of low salivary flow among asthmatic children, and its persistence as a significant independent predictor after multivariable adjustment (OR = 4.017, 95% CI: 1.443–11.178, p = 0.008), suggests that asthma and its pharmacological management may compromise salivary gland function through mechanisms that are not explained by behavioral factors alone []. Kargul et al. similarly reported decreased salivary and plaque pH in asthmatic children using inhalers, further supporting the potential role of reduced salivary protection in this population [].

Although overall OHRQoL scores were generally low in both groups, suggesting a relatively favorable oral health-related quality of life, asthmatic children consistently reported higher SOHO-5 scores compared with non-asthmatic peers in the bivariate analysis. These differences were most pronounced in functional domains such as eating and speaking, which may reflect the combined burden of oral and respiratory symptoms on daily functioning. Comparable scores were observed in a study conducted in a healthy school population, where mean total SOHO-5 scores were 1.86 ± 2.27 for child self-report and 2.65 ± 3.13 for parental report [], suggesting that the scores observed in our control group are consistent with population norms. By contrast, Abanto et al. reported higher mean scores in both child (3.32 ± 3.22) and parent versions (5.18 ± 6.28) in a Brazilian school population [], highlighting the variability in OHRQoL scores across different populations and healthcare contexts.

After multivariable adjustment, however, the association between asthma and OHRQoL was attenuated and did not reach statistical significance, either for child-reported (B = 0.732, p = 0.090) or total scores (B = 0.693, p = 0.293). This suggests that the observed bivariate differences in OHRQoL may be partly explained by confounders such as pain experience and dietary habits rather than by asthma alone. The discrepancy between child and parent-reported scores is also noteworthy: parents consistently underestimated the oral health burden compared with their children’s self-assessments, reinforcing the importance of incorporating child-reported outcomes in both research and clinical practice []. Reliance on parental proxy reports alone may therefore mask the true impact of oral conditions on children’s daily lives.

Dental pain emerged as the strongest predictor of OHRQoL across all multivariable models (SOHO-5 child: B = −1.583, p = 0.006; SOHO-5 total: B = −4.970, p < 0.001), in some cases outweighing the contribution of asthma itself. This finding underscores the importance of preventive strategies and timely management of dental caries in all children, and particularly in those with chronic respiratory conditions such as asthma, who may face additional barriers to oral healthcare access. Subgroup analyses further suggested that asthmatic children with additional risk factors—namely caries in permanent teeth and low salivary flow—reported markedly poorer OHRQoL, although these findings should be interpreted with caution given the small cell sizes involved.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and the relatively small sample size, though justified by an a priori power analysis, may have limited the detection of more subtle associations, particularly in subgroup analyses; therefore, stratified findings should be interpreted with caution and considered exploratory. The non-probabilistic convenience sampling from two different settings, a hospital immunoallergology service and a primary school, may introduce systematic differences in socioeconomic status and healthcare utilization between groups, which may limit the comparability between groups.

Notably, significant differences in parental education were observed between groups, suggesting that socioeconomic confounding may not have been fully addressed despite the multivariable adjustment conducted, and residual confounding cannot be excluded. The multivariable analyses were also constrained by the available sample size, limiting the number of covariates that could be included while maintaining adequate event-per-variable ratios. Additionally, parental reports of oral health behaviors may be subject to recall or social desirability bias. Finally, dietary habits were only partially assessed.

Despite these limitations, this study provides novel insights into an important but underexplored area. To our knowledge, it is the first study to specifically examine the association between asthma and OHRQoL in children aged 6 to 8 years using a child self-report instrument in a Portuguese population. By focusing on this developmental stage, when both primary and permanent dentition coexist, the study captures a critical window of vulnerability for oral health. The asthma diagnosis was established by pediatric immunoallergologists with clinical experience, ensuring diagnostic accuracy. The use of a validated and culturally adapted Portuguese version of the SOHO-5, with demonstrated internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.86) and temporal reliability (ICC = 0.82), ensures methodological rigor and comparability with international research. The integration of both clinical indicators and child-reported quality-of-life assessments, together with the inclusion of multivariable analyses, represents a key methodological strength of this study. The inclusion of pain experience as a covariate in multivariable models represents an additional methodological strength, as this variable emerged as the dominant predictor of OHRQoL and its omission could have led to overestimation of the effect of asthma.

The findings of this study highlight several directions for future research. First, longitudinal studies with larger and matched samples are needed to establish causal pathways between asthma, its pharmacological management, and oral health outcomes, as well as to assess changes over time in both salivary function and OHRQoL. Second, future studies should incorporate comprehensive dietary assessment, including sugar intake frequency and quantity, to better disentangle the contributions of asthma and behavioral risk factors to caries experience in this population. Third, matched study designs or multivariable approaches with adequate sample sizes would allow for more robust control of socioeconomic confounders, particularly parental education and healthcare access.

Finally, given that low salivary flow was the only oral health outcome for which asthma remained a significant independent predictor after multivariable adjustment, future studies should specifically investigate the role of inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators on salivary gland function, including objective measures of salivary composition and buffering capacity.

Within the limitations of this cross-sectional study, children with asthma exhibited a higher caries burden and a significantly higher prevalence of low stimulated salivary flow compared with non-asthmatic peers. After multivariable adjustment, asthma remained a significant independent predictor of low salivary flow, while the association with caries was attenuated and no longer statistically significant, suggesting partial confounding by dietary habits. Dental pain emerged as the primary determinant of OHRQoL, and child-reported outcomes consistently captured a greater burden than parental proxy reports. These findings underscore the importance of integrating oral health surveillance into the routine care of asthmatic children, with particular attention paid to salivary function and caries prevention.

This cross-sectional study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Dental Medicine, University of Lisbon (reference: 202326, Approval date: 27 November 2023) and the Ethics Committee of São José Local Health Unit (reference: 1512/2024, Approval date: 8 May 2024).

Informed written consent was obtained from all parents or legal guardians of the participating children prior to enrolment in the study. Given the age of the study population (6 to 8 years), verbal assent was additionally obtained from the children themselves, in accordance with ethical guidelines for research involving minors. All data were fully anonymized prior to analysis. No identifying information is included in this manuscript.

The data presented in this study are not publicly available due to ethical restrictions and privacy considerations related to the participation of minor subjects. Data may be available upon reasonable request to the corresponding author (S.V.M.), subject to ethical approval by the relevant institutional committees.

title: Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation in acute asthmatic attack.
abstract: Asthma is characterised by reversible airway obstruction. In most patients, control of disease activity is easily achieved. However, in a small minority, asthma may be fatal. Between the two extremes lie patients with severe asthmatic attacks, refractory to standard treatment. These patients are at an increased risk of recurrent severe attacks, with respiratory failure, and mechanical ventilation. Invasive mechanical ventilation of the asthmatic patient is associated with a higher risk of complications and, therefore, is a measure of last resort. Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV) is another treatment modality that may be beneficial in patients with severe asthmatic attack who are at an increased risk of developing respiratory failure. These patients have the potential to benefit from early respiratory support in the form of NPPV. However, reports of NPPV in asthmatic patients are scarce, and its usage in asthmatic attacks is, therefore, still controversial. Only a few reports of NPPV in asthma have been published over the last decade. These studies mostly involve small numbers of patients and those who have problematic methodology. In this article we review the available evidence for NPPV in asthma and try to formulate our recommendations for NPPV application in asthma based on the available evidence and reports.

These patients are at an increased risk of recurrent severe attacks, with respiratory failure, and mechanical ventilation. Invasive mechanical ventilation of the asthmatic patient is associated with a higher risk of complications and, therefore, is a measure of last resort. Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV) is another treatment modality that may be beneficial in patients with severe asthmatic attack who are at an increased risk of developing respiratory failure. These patients have the potential to benefit from early respiratory support in the form of NPPV. However, reports of NPPV in asthmatic patients are scarce, and its usage in asthmatic attacks is, therefore, still controversial. Only a few reports of NPPV in asthma have been published over the last decade. These studies mostly involve small numbers of patients and those who have problematic methodology. In this article we review the available evidence for NPPV in asthma and try to formulate our recommendations for NPPV application in asthma based on the available evidence and reports.

title: Asthma onset pattern and patient outcomes in a chronic rhinosinusitis population.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is strongly associated with comorbid asthma. This study compares early-onset and late-onset asthma in a CRS population using patient-reported and clinical characteristics. METHODS: At enrollment into a clinical registry, CRS patients completed the 22-item Sino-Nasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22), Asthma Control Test (ACT), mini-Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire (miniAQLQ), the 29-item Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS-29), and medication use questionnaires. Patients also reported comorbid asthma and age at first asthma diagnosis. Early-onset (<18 years) and late-onset (>18 years) asthma groups were defined. Analysis of variance (ANOVA), chi-square, and Kruskal-Wallis tests were used to compare patient responses. RESULTS: A total of 199 non-asthmatic (56.1%), 71 early-onset asthmatic (20.0%), and 85 late-onset asthmatic (23.9%) CRS patients completed the survey. Body mass index (BMI) was significantly higher in late-onset asthmatic (p = 0.046) while age, gender, race, and smoking history did not differ with time of asthma onset. SNOT-22, ACT, and miniAQLQ were not different between asthma groups, but late-onset asthmatics had significantly lower physical function than non-asthmatics (p = 0.008). Compared to non-asthmatics, late-onset asthmatics showed increased rates of nasal polyps (p < 0.001), higher Lund-Mackay scores (p = 0.005), and had received more oral steroid courses (p < 0.001) and endoscopic surgeries (p = 0.008) for CRS management. Late-onset asthmatics compared to early-onset asthmatics showed increased nasal polyposis (p = 0.011) and oral steroid courses for CRS (p = 0.003). CONCLUSION: While CRS-specific and asthma-specific patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) were not significantly different among groups, CRS patients with late-onset asthma had poorer physical function, more frequent nasal polyposis, and required increased treatment for CRS. Late-onset asthma may predict more severe disease in CRS.

title: MyD88 mediates allergic airway inflammation by regulating ILC2s function through inducing the formation of P38/GATA3 complex.
abstract: BackgroundAllergic asthma stands as the predominant asthma phenotype propelled by aberrant type 2 immune response. Type-2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) are significant for generating IL-5 and IL-13 cytokines, highlighting their vital role in triggering and escalating the progression of asthma. Myeloid differentiation primary response protein 88 (MyD88) controls innate and adaptive immune responses by orchestrating inflammatory signals.ObjectiveThis work focused on investigating the influence of MyD88 in governing ILC2s-driven allergic airway disease alongside its underlying molecular mechanisms.MethodsWe evaluated the effects of MyD88 in IL-33-induced or allergen-induced airway hyperreactivity (AHR) and airway inflammation. The role and mechanism of MyD88 in regulating ILC2s function were examined in vivo and in vitro by using transcriptome sequencing analysis, flow cytometry, clinical samples, ILC2-specific MyD88 knockout mice, and anti-Thy1.2 antibody against ILC2s in mice.ResultsThe results showed heightened MyD88 expression in ILC2s sourced from allergic asthmatic patients and asthmatic mice. MyD88 knockout in ILC2s was able to mitigate IL-33-induced airway inflammation, while the MyD88 inhibitor LM8 proves efficacious in attenuating allergen-induced airway inflammation and AHR. After elimination of ILC2s via anti-Thy1.2 antibody, the pharmacological activity of LM8 diminished. Mechanistic studies revealed that MyD88 mediates the activation and proliferation of ILC2s through facilitation of P38-GATA3 complex formation.ConclusionsThe research highlights MyD88 as a critical regulator of ILC2s activation, suggesting its potential utility as a therapeutic target for interventions in allergic asthma.

sections.abstract:
Allergic asthma stands as the predominant asthma phenotype propelled by aberrant type 2 immune response. Type-2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) are significant for generating IL-5 and IL-13 cytokines, highlighting their vital role in triggering and escalating the progression of asthma. Myeloid differentiation primary response protein 88 (MyD88) controls innate and adaptive immune responses by orchestrating inflammatory signals.

This work focused on investigating the influence of MyD88 in governing ILC2s-driven allergic airway disease alongside its underlying molecular mechanisms.

We evaluated the effects of MyD88 in IL-33-induced or allergen-induced airway hyperreactivity (AHR) and airway inflammation. The role and mechanism of MyD88 in regulating ILC2s function were examined in vivo and in vitro by using transcriptome sequencing analysis, flow cytometry, clinical samples, ILC2-specific MyD88 knockout mice, and anti-Thy1.2 antibody against ILC2s in mice.

The results showed heightened MyD88 expression in ILC2s sourced from allergic asthmatic patients and asthmatic mice. MyD88 knockout in ILC2s was able to mitigate IL-33-induced airway inflammation, while the MyD88 inhibitor LM8 proves efficacious in attenuating allergen-induced airway inflammation and AHR. After elimination of ILC2s via anti-Thy1.2 antibody, the pharmacological activity of LM8 diminished. Mechanistic studies revealed that MyD88 mediates the activation and proliferation of ILC2s through facilitation of P38-GATA3 complex formation.

The research highlights MyD88 as a critical regulator of ILC2s activation, suggesting its potential utility as a therapeutic target for interventions in allergic asthma.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12931-026-03746-8.
sections.other:
Asthma presents as a heterogeneous disease characterized by diverse manifestations including persistent airway inflammation, airway hyper-responsiveness (AHR), and airway remodeling []. Within the spectrum of asthma types, allergic asthma emerges as the most common phenotype []. Its onset typically occurs during childhood, with a notable increase in frequency observed throughout childhood and adolescence []. Currently, inhaled corticosteroids (ICSs) are the cornerstone therapy for allergic asthma management. However, adherence to ICS-containing medications for daily maintenance remains suboptimal among patients. Even with maximal adherence to standard-of-care controller therapy, a significant proportion of asthma patients continue to experience uncontrolled symptoms [, ]. Consequently, it is imperative to identify new treatment targets and establish effective protocols in order to ensure optimal control of this condition.

The traditional model, which focuses on type 2 T helper (Th2) cell-mediated B cell production of immunoglobulin E (IgE), activation of mast cells, and recruitment of eosinophils, has been the central framework for understanding allergic asthma []. Yet, this framework does not fully explain the disease’s pathophysiology. Emerging evidence has highlighted the critical role of Type-2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s), originating from common lymphoid progenitors, in asthma’s onset and progression []. Regulated by transcription factor GATA-binding protein 3 (GATA3), ILC2s respond robustly to epithelial cell, macrophage, and dendritic cell (DC) derived cytokines and mediators, notably through the ST2 receptor [, ]. Triggered by interleukin (IL)−33, IL-25, and thymic stromal lymphopoietin, ILC2s significantly contribute to the production of Th2 cytokines, fundamental to the pathology of allergic diseases [, ]. In respiratory contexts, ILC2s lead to pulmonary eosinophilia and AHR triggered by allergens such as Alternaria alternata (Alt), independent of B and T cell involvement [, ], and have been implicated in corticosteroid-resistant asthma []. Therefore, understanding the molecular mechanisms of ILC2 activation and its mediation of inflammatory responses is crucial for grasping the pathological processes of allergic asthma.

Myeloid differentiation primary response protein 88 (MyD88) serves as a critical adaptor protein of the toll like receptor (TLR) family, except for TLR3, and IL-1 receptor, orchestrating innate and adaptive immune responses by transducing inflammatory signals [–]. Previous study has demonstrated a significantly heightened expression of MyD88 gene in lung tissue extracted from mice with allergic asthma induced by ovalbumin (OVA)/lipopolysaccharide, compared to controls []. Furthermore, RNA sequencing analysis of peripheral blood samples revealed notable upregulation of MyD88 among the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in children with asthma compared with healthy individuals []. MyD88 signaling is indispensable in several cell types within lung tissue for the development of asthma, inhibition of which has been shown to alleviate allergic airway inflammation and AHR [–]. However, a comprehensive understanding of MyD88’s expression and function in ILC2s under the asthmatic condition, as well as the mechanisms by which it influences inflammation driven by ILC2s in the airways, remains to be fully elucidated.

In this study, samples obtained from both asthma patients and animal models induced by IL-33 or fungal allergen were utilized. ILC2s, derived from individuals with asthma, exhibited elevated levels of MyD88 expression. Selective ablation of MyD88 in ILC2s resulted in a reduction in the production of type 2 cytokines and conferred protection against airway inflammation in mice. MyD88 inhibitor LM8, synthesized by our group (identified originally as compound 15c) [], significantly attenuated airway inflammation and AHR induced by IL-33 or Alt. The pharmacological activity of LM8 was dependent on the presence of ILC2s, as evidenced by the loss of its efficacy upon ILC2 elimination. Mechanistic studies have found that MyD88 mediates the activation of ILC2s by promoting its downstream P38 to form a complex with GATA3, thereby releasing IL-5 and IL-13. Overall, the data strongly indicate the pivotal role of MyD88 as a critical regulator in ILC2s and also highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for reducing pulmonary inflammation driven by ILC2s.
sections.methods:
LM8, boasting a purity of 98.9%, was dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) for in vitro investigations or mixed with olive oil (Aladdin, China) for in vivo experiments. Recombinant mouse (rm) IL-33 was purchased from Novoprotein (Shanghai, China). Alt extracts were purchased from Greer Laboratories (CA, USA). Recombinant human (rh) IL-33, rhIL-2, rhIL-7, rmIL-2, and rmIL-7 were obtained from Peprotech (NJ, USA). The Foxp3 transcription factor staining kit was purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific (MA, USA). Phorbol 12-Myristate 13-Acetate (PMA)/Ionomycin and Brefeldin A (BFA)/Monensin were purchased from MultiSciences Biotech (Hangzhou, China). Propidium Iodide (PI) was purchased from Beyotime Biological Technology (Shanghai, China). Mouse IL-5 and IL-13 Enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits and TRIZOL reagent were obtained from Invitrogen (CA, USA). Collagenase type IV was obtained from Worthington Biochemical Corp (NJ, USA). DNase I was obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific (MA, USA). The Pierce ECL western blotting substrate was purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific (MA, USA). Human TruStain FcX™ (Fc Receptor Blocking Solution) was purchased from BioLegend (CA, USA). Antibodies used in this study are listed in Table S1.

Following the approval granted by the Institutional Review Board of the Second Affiliated Hospital and Yuying Children's Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University (Approved number: 2023-k-72–02), informed consent was secured from each participant involved in the study. A total of 24 children aged 6 to 14 years were enrolled, with 12 classified as healthy and 12 diagnosed with asthma. The diagnosis of asthma and the corresponding asthma pharmacologic treatment were established in accordance with the criteria of the Global Initiative for Asthma. Regular flow cytometric analysis was performed on a BD LSRFortessa X-20 (BD Biosciences, NJ, USA). The staining procedure was conducted using Alexa Fluor 405-conjugated anti-human MyD88, utilizing the Foxp3 transcription factor staining kit.

Female C57BL/6 mice, 6–8 weeks old, were obtained from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Company. Additionally, B6/JGpt‐MyD88 flox/flox mice (MyD88 f/f Strain NO. T009598) were sourced from GemPharmatech Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, China). This conditional floxed strain was established with two loxP sites specifically flanking exon 2 to exon 6 of the endogenous MyD88 gene via CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing. Six-week-old MyD88 f/f mice were intratracheally (i.t.) administered with 5 × 10 11 adeno-associated virus (AAV6) vectors expressing IL-5 core promoter (AAV6- Il5 cre) to induce MyD88 knockout in ILC2s (Fig. S1). All mice were maintained in a controlled environment at the animal facility of Wenzhou Medical University, adhering to a stringent 12-h light/dark regimen. Prior to the commencement of experiments, the mice underwent a minimum acclimatization period of two weeks within the laboratory environment. Mouse protocols were approved by the Wenzhou Medical University Animal Policy and Welfare Committee (Approved No: xmsq2022-1030).

C57BL/6 mice were randomly assigned to three groups: control group (CON), IL-33 model group (IL-33), and LM8 treatment group (IL-33 + LM8). Mice in the IL-33 model and LM8 treatment groups underwent intratracheal challenges with rmIL-33 (0.5 µg per mouse) on days 0, 1, 2, and 3. In the LM8 treatment group, mice were intraperitoneally ( i.p. ) injected with LM8 solution (10 mg/kg each mouse) 30 min prior to IL-33 challenge. Mice in the control group received challenges with phosphate buffered saline (PBS). MyD88 f/f + AAV6- Il5 cre mice and MyD88 f/f + AAV6-CON mice were employed to establish models of IL-33-induced airway inflammation and AHR. To target ILC2s for depletion in C57BL/6 mice, i.p. injections of Anti-Thy1.2 (200 μg per mouse in 100 μL PBS) or IgG1 isotype control antibody were administered on days −6, −4, −1, 0, and 2.

C57BL/6 mice were randomly assigned to three groups: control group (CON), Alt model group (Alt), LM8 treatment group (Alt + LM8). Those designated to the Alt model and LM8 treatment groups underwent intratracheal challenges with Alt extracts (5 μg per mouse) on days 0, 1, 2, and 3. In the LM8 treatment group, mice received intraperitoneal injections of the LM8 solution (10 mg/kg each mouse) 30 min prior to Alt challenge. Mice in the control group were subjected to challenges with PBS.

Lung resistance (Rn) measurements were conducted on anesthetized, tracheostomized mice using the FlexiVent system (SCIREQ, Canada). The protocol included initial exposures to aerosolized saline (baseline) followed by escalating doses (3.125, 6.25, 12.5, 25, and 50 mg/mL) of methacholine for sequential challenges []. Rn was recorded at each dose to ascertain the percentage change relative to the baseline.

A tracheal cannula was inserted into the primary bronchus to facilitate BALF collection. The procedure included infusion of cold PBS through the cannula, as previously described []. For eosinophil identification in experiments, we utilized a series of antibodies including PerCP anti-mouse CD45, APC anti-mouse CD11b, PE-cy7 anti-mouse Ly6G, and PE anti-mouse Siglec-F, as detailed in the schematic of Figure S2 []. Lung tissue from C57BL/6 mice were surgically removed, finely minced, and then subjected to digestion in RPMI-1640 (Gibco/BRL life Technologies, Eggenstein, Germany) containing 1 mg/mL type IV collagenase and 20 U/mL DNase I, maintained at 37 °C for one hour. This process was followed by mechanical disaggregation of the tissue, followed by filtration through a 70-μm cell strainer. To lyse residual red blood cells (RBCs), the remaining pellet was then treated with 1 × RBC lysis buffer (Solarbio Science & Technology, Beijing, China). The pellet was subsequently undergoing additional processing to enable flow cytometry analysis []. The prepared single-cell suspensions were first blocked with anti-CD16/CD32 to reduce non-specific staining, before being labeled with fluorescent antibodies specifically targeting ILC2 markers: PerCP-Cy5.5 anti-mouse lineage cocktail (CD3e, CD11b, CD45R/B220, TER-119, Ly-6G, and Ly-6C), BB515 anti-mouse CD45, PE anti-mouse ST2, and APC anti-mouse CD127. 7AAD staining was employed to exclude dead cells. The detailed gating strategies used are depicted in Figure S3A. For intranuclear staining, we applied BV421 anti-mouse GATA3 and AF405 anti-mouse MyD88, utilizing the Foxp3 transcription factor staining kit. Additionally, for evaluating cytokine production, cells were incubated with PE anti-mouse IL-13 following a 4-h exposure to 1 × PMA/Ionomycin and 1 × BFA/Monensin in complete RPMI-1640. Flow cytometric was conducted on a BD LSRFortessa X-20 (BD Biosciences, NJ, USA), and the data were analyzed with FlowJo software version 10 (CA, USA).

The cells were purified using Fluorescence Activated Cell Sorting (FACS), specifically employing the Moflo Astrios EQ instrument from Beckman Coulter (CA, USA), and achieving a purity level exceeding 95%. Throughout the investigation, ILC2s obtained from wild-type mice were categorized as naïve (nILC2s). Conversely, ILC2s obtained from mice exposed to IL-33 or stimulated with IL-33 in a laboratory setting were categorized as activated (aILC2s) []. The isolated murine ILC2s were incubated at 37 °C in RPMI-1640 medium, which was enriched with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 2% penicillin–streptomycin, and supplemented with rmIL-2 (10 ng/mL) and rmIL-7 (10 ng/mL). In parallel experiments, Naïve ILC2s were subjected to stimulation using 10 ng/mL of rmIL-33 for 24 h in vitro. Human blood samples, sourced from healthy donors of both genders, were processed by treating with 1 × RBC lysis buffer. Human ILC2s in peripheral blood were identified as Lin − FceR1 − CRTH2 + CD127 + cells. The FITC-conjugated anti-human lineage cocktail for human cells included antibodies targeting CD2, CD4, CD14, CD16, CD19, CD56 and CD235a. Additional staining to characterize human ILC2s involved FITC anti-human FceR1, AF647 anti-human CRTH2 and PE anti-human CD127. Cultured human ILC2s were maintained in complete RPMI-1640, supplemented as required with rhIL-2 (20 ng/mL), rhIL-7 (20 ng/mL), and/or rhIL-33 (10 ng/mL), with some experiments also incorporating LM8. Levels of IL-5 and IL-13 secreted into the supernatants were measured using ELISA.

Transcriptome sequencing analysis was conducted on fresh lung tissues from mice by Lianchuan Bio Technologies (Zhejiang, China). The sequencing was conducted on an Illumina Novaseq 6000 platform system (CA, USA), utilizing paired-end reads that were 150 bp in length on each end. Subsequent bioinformatic analysis of the transcriptome sequencing data, which were deposited at GEO (accession number: GSE269435 ), was performed by Lianchuan Bio Technologies (Zhejiang, China).

Total RNA was extracted from lung tissues using TRIZOL reagent, with concentrations subsequently measured through ultraviolet (UV) absorbance at the 260 nm and 280 nm wavelengths. Following extraction, reverse transcription was conducted utilizing HiScript III RT SuperMix (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). For gene expression analysis, SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Nanjing, China) was applied in a QuantStudio™ 3 Real-Time PCR System (Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany) to quantify mRNA levels of Il5 and Il13 . Primers specifically designed for these cytokine genes, provided by Invitrogen (Shanghai, China), are listed in Table S2. The relative expression of these genes was then normalized against the expression of the housekeeping gene Actb to ensure accurate quantification.

Concentrations of IL-5 and IL-13 in lung homogenates, BALF, and cell supernatants were determined using ELISA kits, following the guidelines provided by the kit manufacturers. Following plate blocking, 100 μL of samples were introduced to an ELISA plate coated with monoclonal capture antibodies. The plate underwent a two-hour incubation at ambient temperature. Following this incubation, the plate was subjected to five successive washes with PBST (PBS solution containing 0.1% Tween-20). After the washing steps, detection antibodies, which were conjugated with horseradish peroxidase, were applied to the plate. It was then incubated for an additional hour at room temperature. Post-incubation, the plate was washed again and the detection reaction was initiated using tetramethyl benzidine as a substrate. To halt the enzymatic reaction, 2 M H 2 SO 4 was added. Absorbance was then measured at dual wavelengths of 450 nm and 570 nm utilizing the SpectraMax® iD3 (CA, USA). A standard calibration curve was established using the purified proteins included with the ELISA kit.

After the mice were euthanized, the middle lobe of the right lung was quickly excised and immediately immersed in 4% paraformaldehyde for fixation. The fixed tissue was left overnight in the fixative, then embedded in paraffin. Sections of 4 µm thickness were cut and stained using both Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) and Periodic Acid Schiff (PAS) kit according to established protocols. Histological images were captured using a Nikon microscope (Tokyo, Japan) and analyzed with Image J software (National Institutes of Health, MD, USA).

Isolated murine lung ILC2s were centrifuged at 500 × g for five minutes. The resulting cell pellet was resuspended in 1 × Fixation/Permeabilization solution and incubated for 1–2 h. For intracellular staining, these cells were mounted on microscope slides that had been pre-coated with Poly-D-lysine. The slides were treated with 2% bovine serum albumin in PBS for one hour to block non-specific binding. Overnight incubation with a P38 (1:50) primary antibody was performed at 4 °C. Subsequently, the slides were incubated with AF488-conjugated rabbit IgG (1:200) and BV421-conjugated anti-mouse GATA3 antibodies for one hour at room temperature. The sections were then counterstained with PI (1:50) for 30 min. Imaging was conducted using an epi-fluorescence microscope (Nikon, Tokyo, Japan) to capture the stained samples.

Protein extractions from biological tissues were carried out using Radio Immunoprecipitation Assay buffer (Beyotime Biological Technology, Shanghai, China). These extracts, each comprising approximately 60 μg of proteins, were separated by electrophoresis on a 10% sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel. Following the separation, the proteins were meticulously transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride membranes (Bio-Rad Laboratories Inc, CA, USA). To minimize non-specific protein interactions, these membranes were incubated in a blocking buffer containing Tris-buffered saline, 5% non-fat milk, and Tween-20 for 1.5 h at room temperature. Primary antibody incubation was conducted overnight at 4 °C to ensure optimal binding. The following day, membranes were exposed to horseradish peroxide-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1–2 h at room temperature to facilitate detection. The protein bands were then visualized using an advanced chemiluminescence reagent.

Human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293 T cells, procured from Shanghai Institute of Biochemistry and Cell Biology (Shanghai, China), were cultivated in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium enhanced with 25 mM D-glucose, 10% FBS, and 2% penicillin–streptomycin mixture. To investigate the interaction between P38 and GATA3 following LM8 exposure, cells were genetically modified using the pCMV-HA-GATA3 vector (Sino Biological, Beijing, China) via polyethylenimine (Sigma-Aldrich, MO, USA) mediated transfection. Proteins were then extracted from the cells utilizing a lysis buffer that incorporated a protease inhibitor cocktail tailored for immunoprecipitation (IP) purposes. The cellular extracts were incubated with targeted antibodies overnight at 4 °C, followed by a subsequent 2-h incubation with A/G Sepharose beads at the same temperature to facilitate antibody binding. Post-binding, the beads were rigorously washed five times with 1 × PBS. Proteins were eluted from the beads using SDS loading buffer heated to 100 °C and then subjected to immunoblot analysis to detect and identify specific protein interactions.

The data were analyzed using the program GraphPad Prism 9.0. Values are shown as the mean ± standard error of measurement (SEM). The student’s t-test or One-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), followed by Dunn's post hoc test, were utilized to examine the disparities across the data sets. A p-value less than 0.05 was deemed significant and indicated by either an asterisk (*), a pound symbol ( # ), or a triangle ( △ ).
sections.results:
To investigate the potential molecular regulators of ILC2s in asthma, we initially analyzed transcriptional profiling data of ILC2 from GEO database ( GSE166081 , GSE154823 , and GSE148539 ), revealing elevated levels of MyD88 mRNA induced by IL-33 (Fig. S3B). Subsequently, we assessed MyD88 expression in ILC2s isolated from peripheral blood samples of asthma patients and healthy individuals, whose genders, ages, or illness severities are listed in Table S3, using flow cytometry. Human ILC2s were identified as Lin − FceR1 − CRTH2 + CD127 + cells (Fig. A and Fig. S3C). Notably, MyD88 expression levels in ILC2s from asthma patients were markedly higher than those observed in healthy individuals (Fig. B). Furthermore, we examined the expression of MyD88 in murine lung-resident ILC2s, identified by flow cytometry as Lin − CD45 + ST2 + CD127 + (Fig. C). Our data revealed significantly elevated MyD88 expression levels in both aILC2s (Fig. D and Fig. S3D) and IL-33-stimulated nILC2s (Fig. E-F). These results indicated that heightened MyD88 expression is associated with activated ILC2s and may contribute to ILC2s-mediated inflammation.

During the process of IL-33-induced airway inflammation, ILC2s are recognized as the predominant source of IL-5 in the lungs. To specifically target gene deletions within ILC2s, Il5 RFP-cre mice have been employed []. To further explore the specific role of MyD88 within ILC2s in vivo, we engineered mice with an ILC2-specific deletion of MyD88. This was achieved by delivering AAV6- Il5 cre vectors directly into the trachea of MyD88 f/f mice (Fig. S4A). Upon challenge with IL-33, MyD88 f/f + AAV6- Il5 cre mice exhibited a marked reduction in total cells present in the BALF compared to control mice (Fig. S4B and Fig. A). MyD88 deficiency in ILC2s resulted in diminished expression of type 2 inflammation-associated cytokines, including IL-5 and IL-13 (Fig. B-D). Histological analysis of the lungs (Fig. E, upper two images) consistently demonstrated that MyD88 deficiency in ILC2s led to thinning of the epithelium (Fig. F) compared to control mice. PAS staining (Fig. E, lower two images) further revealed a decrease in mucus hypersecretion in MyD88 f/f + AAV6- Il5 cre mice compared to controls (Fig. G). Additionally, we observed a reduction in the frequencies and total counts of lung ILC2s in MyD88 f/f + AAV6- Il5 cre mice compared to controls (Fig. H). Collectively, these results indicated that MyD88 in lung ILC2s may play a crucial role in mediating IL-33-induced airway inflammation.

To elucidate the mechanism by which MyD88 mediates IL-33-induced airway inflammation in ILC2s, MyD88 pharmacological inhibitor, LM8, was used. Firstly, we evaluate the impact of LM8 on IL-33-induced airway inflammation and AHR in mice. Mice were i.t. challenged with rmIL-33 or PBS and i.p. injected with LM8 or solvent control on days 0, 1, 2, and 3 (Fig. A). Twenty-four hours after the final intratracheal challenge, airway resistance was measured. As anticipated, LM8 treatment significantly attenuated airway resistance in mice challenged with IL-33, suggesting that the inhibition of MyD88 can suppress IL-33-induced AHR (Fig. B). Histological examination of lung tissues (Fig. C, upper three images) revealed that LM8 treatment markedly reduced IL-33-induced thickening of the epithelium (Fig. D). PAS staining (Fig. C, lower three images) demonstrated a substantial elevation in mucus production in the lungs of mice treated with IL-33 when compared to those receiving LM8 treatment (Fig. E). Furthermore, analyses revealed that the populations of CD45 + leukocytes and eosinophils within the BALF were considerably lower in the group treated with both IL-33 and LM8, in contrast to the group exposed solely to IL-33 (Fig. F-G ) . Additionally, the administration of LM8 led to a marked reduction in the concentrations of IL-5 and IL-13 in the lung tissues and BALF of the mice challenged with IL-33 (Fig. H-J). Flow cytometry analysis revealed that pretreatment with LM8 prior to IL-33 challenge decreased both the percentage (Fig. K and Fig. S5) and total number (Fig. L) of lung ILC2s. These results collectively indicate that MyD88 pharmacological inhibition prevents IL-33-induced AHR and airway inflammation.

To determine if LM8's protective effect against airway inflammation is mediated through ILC2s, we depleted these cells in mice utilizing anti-Thy1.2 antibody (Fig. A-C) []. Consistent with our hypothesis, mice that received the anti-Thy1.2 treatment exhibited significantly milder airway inflammation compared to those in the isotype control group. This improvement was marked by a decrease in the total cell count in the BALF (Fig. D), a reduction in the expression of type 2 cytokines (Fig. E -F), diminished epithelial thickness, and a lower percentage of PAS-positive cells (Fig. G-I). However, the protective effect of LM8 was abolished in mice treated with anti-Thy1.2 antibody (Fig. D-I), suggesting that LM8 exerts its protective activity against IL-33-induced airway inflammation by targeting ILC2s.

To explore the molecular mechanisms by which deficiency or inhibition of MyD88 mitigates IL-33-induced airway inflammation, we examined the effect of MyD88 on the activation of ILC2s. Activated mouse ILC2s were isolated and stimulated ex vivo with LM8 or solvent control (Fig. A). Our results revealed that LM8 significantly reduced the levels of transcription factor GATA3 (Fig. B), a well-known crucial regulator of Th2 cell and ILC2 development [], as well as intracellular IL-13 expression (Fig. C), as assessed by flow cytometry analysis. Moreover, LM8 substantially reduced the levels of IL-5 and IL-13 in the culture supernatants (Fig. D), underscoring the vital role of MyD88 in regulating the activity of ILC2s in mice. To extend these findings to human cells, we isolated ILC2s from the peripheral blood of healthy donors using FACS. These cells were cultured in a medium supplemented with rhIL-2, rhIL-7, rhIL-33, and subsequently stimulated ex vivo with either LM8 or a solvent control (Fig. E). After a 48-h period, there was a notable decrease in the secretion of IL-5 and IL-13 in the IL-33-stimulated human ILC2s that received LM8 treatment (Fig. F), aligning with the results observed in mouse ILC2s. These collective findings confirm MyD88 as a critical molecular regulator in the activation process of ILC2s.

To delve deeper into the molecular mechanisms underlying MyD88-mediated ILC2 activation, we conducted transcriptome sequencing on mouse lung tissues. Our analysis revealed 2,251 upregulated and 1,317 downregulated DEGs in response to IL-33 challenge, while 313 upregulated and 895 downregulated DEGs were identified when IL-33-challenged mice were i.p. injected with LM8 (Fig. S6A-C). Notably, 935 DEGs were found to be commonly regulated (Fig. S6D). Pathway analysis of these 935 DEGs was performed using KEGG (Fig. A), highlighting the MAPK signaling pathway, a classic downstream of MyD88, piqued our interest. Western blot analysis demonstrated that LM8 significantly inhibited IL-33-induced phosphorylation of P38 levels in mouse lung tissue, while showing no obvious effects on the phosphorylation of JNK and ERK (Fig. B and Fig. S6E-F). To elucidate the involvement of P38 in IL-33-induced ILC2s activation, the specific inhibitor of P38, SB203580, was used ex vivo (Fig. C). Treatment with SB203580 results in a significant decrease in the expression levels of GATA3 and intracellular IL-13 in aILC2s (Fig. D-E). Moreover, the production of Th2 inflammatory cytokines, both IL-5 and IL-13, was significantly reduced in the culture supernatants of SB203580-treated aILC2s (Fig. F). Altogether, these results indicated that MyD88 regulates the activation of ILC2s via the P38 signaling pathway.

Reports indicated that inhibiting P38 prevents both the phosphorylation of GATA3 and the binding of GATA3 to the promoters of IL-5 and IL-13 [, ]. Immunofluorescence staining assays revealed the expression of P38 in both cytoplasm and nucleus, with colocalization observed with GATA3 in the nucleus of lung ILC2s (Fig. G). Additionally, it was observed that P38 could form a complex with GATA3 in 293 T cells transfected with GATA3 (Fig. H, IP blots, lane 2), while pretreatment with LM8 or SB203580 could inhibit the formation of this complex (Fig. H, IP blots, lane 3 and 4). Furthermore, LM8 or SB203580 pretreatment inhibited the phosphorylation of P38 in 293 T cells (Fig. H). These results strongly support the involvement of P38-GATA3 interactions in the control of MyD88-mediated ILC2s activation.

We then assessed the therapeutic efficacy of LM8 in a model of AHR and lung inflammation that was clinically relevant, induced by the fungal allergen Alt [, ]. For this purpose, mice received i.t. challenged with either Alt or PBS daily for four consecutive days. Additionally, they were administered LM8 or a solvent control intraperitoneally 30 min prior to each Alt exposure (Fig. A). Our findings revealed that LM8 effectively suppressed Alt-induced AHR in mice (Fig. B). Furthermore, results showed that LM8 treatment significantly reduced epithelial thickness and the number of PAS + cells, as assessed by H&E staining and PAS staining, respectively (Fig. C-E). In addition, Alt-induced type 2 inflammation were suppressed, as evidenced by reduced levels of BALF CD45 + leukocytes and eosinophil infiltration (Fig. F-G), as well as decreased levels of lung IL-5 and IL-13 (Fig. H-I), in LM8-treated mice. Flow cytometric analysis further confirmed that LM8 treatment ameliorated the percentages (Fig. J and Fig. S7A) and numbers (Fig. S7B) of lung ILC2s. These results collectively demonstrate that pharmacologic inhibition of MyD88 attenuates Alt-induced AHR and type 2 inflammation.
sections.discussion:
This work elucidated the pivotal role and underlying mechanism of MyD88 in the context of ILC2s-induced allergic airway inflammation and AHR, suggesting the potential of MyD88 as a target for asthma treatment. We observed elevated levels of MyD88 in ILC2s derived from both asthma patients and asthmatic mice. Our findings demonstrated the indispensable role of MyD88 in ILC2s activation and airway inflammation, as evidenced by MyD88 knockout in ILC2s, which leads to a reduced ILC2s activity. Furthermore, we revealed that inhibition of MyD88 by LM8 yielded similar results to MyD88 knockout in ILC2s, with the pharmacological activity of LM8 disappearing upon ILC2s elimination. Mechanistically, P38 mediates MyD88-induced ILC2s activation by directly interacting with GATA3. Further, pharmacological inhibition of MyD88 alleviated Alt-induced airway inflammation and AHR in mice.

Allergic or environmental insults trigger physical and functional airway epithelial damage, disrupting the epithelial barrier and driving the release and proteolytic maturation of epithelial-derived alarmins, including IL-33, as well as inflammasome-dependent processing of pro-IL-1β [, ]. Both alarmins are commonly involved in allergic airway responses, whereas IL-33 serves as the predominant and direct activator of lung-resident ILC2s to trigger type 2 inflammatory cascades [, ]. At the cellular level, the epithelial-derived alarmin axis acts as a primary upstream inflammatory signal, and multiple lung-resident immune cells further amplify inflammatory microenvironment to facilitate ILC2 activation []. At the molecular level, IL-33 binds specifically to the surface ST2 receptor of ILC2s to initiate intracellular signaling cascades []. Upon activation, ILC2 cells not only proliferate rapidly but also secrete higher levels of Th2 cytokines, including IL-13 and IL-5, which are essential for progression of allergic airway inflammation and asthma pathogenesis [, ]. Although epithelial injury concurrently induces the maturation of IL-1β, the present study specifically focuses on the IL-33-mediated inflammatory cascade; thus, pure IL-33 stimulation was applied both in vitro and in vivo to exclusively dissect the regulatory mechanism governing IL-33-driven ILC2 activation.

A broad array of factors has been identified that influence the activation of ILC2s and their cytokine production during such inflammation, encompassing regulatory cytokines, hormones, growth factors, complement peptides, neuropeptides, neurotransmitters, and lipid mediators []. Previous studies have clarified the molecular mechanisms underlying IL-33-induced ILC2 activation: the alarmin cytokine IL-33 triggers a translocation of STAT3 into the mitochondria to promote adenosine triphosphate synthesis and ILC2 activation []; meanwhile, the STING/IFN-I signaling also mediates IL-33-induced proliferation and activation of ILC2 cells []. However, a comprehensive understanding of the regulatory mechanisms governing ILC2s function remains elusive, and whether a intrinsic signaling molecule regulates ILC2 activation has not been fully elucidated. Hence, MyD88, a central component of the classic innate immunity system, has emerged as a key signaling molecule within TLR pathways, proving indispensable for the induction of adaptive Th1 and Th2 immunity [, ]. MyD88 is present in various lung-resident and immune cells, including DCs, T cells, epithelial cells, and CD11c-positive myeloid cells [, ]. Studies by Ro M et al. have demonstrated the role of MyD88 in the IL-33-induced production of IL-13 in mast cells []. Moreover, intrinsic MyD88 signaling in B cells is crucial for the IgE response to pollen allergens in the lungs []. Contrarily, evidence from another study suggests that MyD88 signaling is not necessary for the generation of IL-17 from ST2 + ILC2s in the lungs in response to IL-33 [], suggesting the cell-specific functional heterogeneity. Our research observed a marked increase in MyD88 expression specifically in ILC2s following IL-33 stimulation.

Agoro R et al. reported the significant role of ILC2s in papain-induced lung inflammation, while MyD88-dependent signaling in T cells, epithelial cells, myeloid cells, and DCs does not contribute to the inflammatory responses to papain []. Thus, we speculate that MyD88-dependent signaling in ILC2s may contribute to the ILC2s-mediated inflammation. Previous studies showed that IL-33 can robustly induce ILC2s-mediated airway inflammation and AHR in mouse model, entirely independent of the acquired immune system [, , ]. Our results showed that the deficiency of MyD88 in lung ILC2s prevents airway inflammation in response to IL-33, indicating that MyD88 in ILC2s mediates IL-33-induced airway inflammation. Moreover, administration of LM8 effectively prevented IL-33-induced AHR, eosinophilia, and secretion of Th2 cytokines, and its pharmacological activity in vivo requires targeting ILC2s. In addition, LM8 suppressed the activation and expansion of ILC2s induced by IL-33.

When MyD88 is recruited to receptors on the cell membrane, it activates downstream MAPK and NF-κB signaling pathways, thus inducing an inflammatory response 17 . Our transcriptome sequencing results revealed significant enrichment of DEGs in the lung tissue in the MAPK signaling pathway. We then confirmed that LM8 significantly inhibited IL-33-induced phosphorylation of P38 signaling. P38 signaling has been reported to regulate cytokines production in IL-33 stimulated ILC2s from mesenteric fat []. Our results further clarified that MyD88 mediated IL-33-induced activation of pulmonary ILC2s via the P38 signaling pathway. It is well-established that GATA3, acting as a master transcriptional regulator, is essential for IL-5 and IL-13 production in ILC2s []. Our study showed that P38 directly binds to GATA3 by co-immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence assays. Our work detailed the molecular mechanisms of MyD88 in the development of IL-33-induced allergic airway inflammation, wherein MyD88 controls the ability of ILC2s to directly respond to IL-33 and produce type 2 cytokines by influencing the formation of P38/GATA3 complex.

Alt is one of the most common inhalation allergens and is closely associated with asthma []. Therefore, the clinical significance of MyD88 in this inflammatory condition was further validated by utilizing an Alt-induced asthma model. Our results showed a novel role for LM8 in ameliorating fungal-allergen-induced airway inflammation and AHR by targeting lung ILC2s. To ensure clinically relevant, we conducted further validation of our results in human ILC2s, recognizing the utility of mice asthma models in elucidating immunologic mechanisms. Studies have documented a significant increase in the expression of MyD88 in asthmatic patients [, ]. Our results indicated that increased expression of MyD88 is indicative of ILC2s activation in asthma patients. Here, we investigated the impact of MyD88-dependent stimulation of human ILC2s and demonstrated that MyD88 inhibition reduced the production of type 2 cytokine in activated human ILC2s, consistent with our findings in mice.

In conclusion, MyD88 is highly expressed in ILC2s and regulates their ability to directly respond to IL-33 and produce type 2 cytokines, achieved through modulation of the formation of the P38/GATA3 complex. Our data unequivocally demonstrated that LM8, a small molecule inhibitor of MyD88, reduced the expression of GATA3 and type 2 cytokine production in ILC2s, thereby attenuating allergic airway inflammation. Given the inherent risk of impaired host antimicrobial resistance caused by global MyD88 suppression, non-ablative and moderate MyD88 inhibition may serve as a feasible intervention strategy for ILC2-dependent allergic asthma. Notably, translational application should fully consider immune homeostasis and potential immunological side effects. Taken together, our results suggest that MyD88 in ILC2s plays an important role in the development of allergic airway inflammation.

title: Genetic predisposition to elevated total immunoglobulin E levels defines a distinct adult-onset-predominant asthma phenotype.
abstract: Asthma heterogeneity remains a major barrier in precision medicine. Although elevated total serum immunoglobulin E (IgE) is a hallmark of asthma, even in nonatopic patients, its causal role in asthma pathogenesis is debated. We hypothesized that genetic predisposition to increased IgE defines a distinct asthma endotype. A genome-wide association study of total serum IgE in 1,287 non-asthmatic Japanese adults was used to construct IgE polygenic risk scores (IgE_PRS). Applying IgE_PRS to 745 patients with asthma, we performed cluster analysis incorporating age at onset, total IgE levels, IgE_PRS, and percent predicted forced expiratory volume in 1 s (pFEV1), identifying four distinct adult asthma phenotypes. Notably, one cluster had the highest IgE_PRS and adult-onset-predominant type 2 inflammation. Conversely, the second cluster displayed the highest IgE levels but average IgE_PRS. The remaining two clusters comprised patients with lower IgE_PRS. One cluster was characterized by eosinophilia and smoking-related airflow limitation, whereas the other exhibited a type 2 low phenotype. In a 10-year retrospective cohort, over 30% of newly diagnosed asthma cases fell into the genetically predisposed high-IgE_PRS cluster. These findings reveal a distinct adult-onset-predominant asthma phenotype driven by genetically determined IgE production, offering new avenues for endotype-driven diagnosis and personalized therapy.
